## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, the enriched biological pathways are ranked according to statistical significance, biological coherence, and likely relevance to kidney disease. Among the strongest signals, inflammatory and innate immune pathways are particularly prominent. The most statistically significant example is neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695, p = 2.88 × 10−16, associated protein count = 89), while the nuclear factor kappa B transcription factor motif (TF:M00194_1, p = 1.49 × 10−3, associated protein count = 44) also appears among the prioritized terms. Taken together, these enrichments suggest that persistent inflammatory activation may represent a central component of the disease biology. This interpretation is broadly consistent with prior literature indicating that nuclear factor kappa B signaling is linked to cytokine production, leukocyte recruitment, and tissue injury in both chronic and acute kidney disorders, whereas neutrophil granule release has been associated with oxidative stress, endothelial injury, and amplification of renal inflammation.

Building on this inflammatory context, the enrichment pattern also extends to pathways related to extracellular matrix remodeling and tissue injury. In particular, degradation of the extracellular matrix (REAC:R-HSA-1474228, p = 1.11 × 10−13, associated protein count = 41) and matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129, p = 4.07 × 10−6, associated protein count = 13) are strongly represented. These findings are relevant because abnormal extracellular matrix turnover is a recognized feature of kidney disease progression and may provide a mechanistic link between inflammatory injury and the development of glomerular and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. In a related manner, the enrichment of actin-based cell projection (GO:0098858, p = 2.97 × 10−2, associated protein count = 17) and late endosome (GO:0005770, p = 4.55 × 10−2, associated protein count = 24) points to possible alterations in cytoskeletal organization and vesicular trafficking. These processes are important for podocyte structure, tubular transport, and protein handling in the kidney, and their appearance here may therefore fit with the broader pattern of tissue injury and structural disruption.

Extending from structural injury to cellular homeostasis, several metabolic and molecular function terms further indicate possible disturbances in lipid and ion handling. These include carboxylic acid binding (GO:0031406, p = 1.94 × 10−8, associated protein count = 30), calcium ion binding (GO:0005509, p = 7.27 × 10−11, associated protein count = 56), phosphatidylcholine metabolic process (GO:0046470, p = 5.70 × 10−4, associated protein count = 13), and fatty acid transport (GO:0015908, p = 4.18 × 10−4, associated protein count = 16). Although these terms are functionally diverse, together they may be compatible with published observations suggesting that calcium dysregulation, lipid metabolic stress, and altered fatty acid handling contribute to tubular cell injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive fibrosis. Finally, disease-oriented enrichments such as rheumatoid arthritis (KEGG:05323, p = 6.08 × 10−8, associated protein count = 25), malaria (KEGG:05144, p = 1.15 × 10−7, associated protein count = 18), amyloidosis (HP:0011034, p = 2.82 × 10−2, associated protein count = 12), and acute ischemic stroke (HP:0002140, p = 3.55 × 10−2, associated protein count = 10) may reflect shared mechanisms involving systemic inflammation, vascular injury, and protein deposition that could also be relevant to renal pathology. Overall, the most significant pathways appear to converge on inflammation, extracellular matrix degradation, cytoskeletal and endosomal dysfunction, and metabolic stress, all of which are broadly supported in the literature as contributors to kidney injury and disease progression.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

With this overall enrichment landscape in view, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### Factor: NF-kappaB; motif: NGGGGAMTTTCCNN; match class: 1 (TF:M00194_1) 

Nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells is a central transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinates cellular responses to inflammatory, infectious, oxidative, metabolic, and hemodynamic stress. The pathway is typically activated by extracellular signals such as tumor necrosis factor, interleukin one, toll-like receptor ligands, advanced glycation end products, angiotensin two, reactive oxygen species, and mechanical injury. In resting cells, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells dimers are retained in the cytoplasm through association with inhibitory proteins of the inhibitor of kappa B family. Upon stimulation, inhibitor of kappa B kinase complexes phosphorylate inhibitor of kappa B proteins, promoting their degradation and allowing nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells to translocate to the nucleus, where it binds cognate deoxyribonucleic acid motifs and induces transcription of genes involved in cytokine production, chemokine expression, leukocyte recruitment, cell survival, adhesion, fibrosis, and innate immune activation. The motif provided here, NGGGGAMTTTCCNN, is consistent with a canonical nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells binding sequence and therefore represents a cis-regulatory element through which this pathway can directly control target gene expression. In the kidney, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells activity is observed in glomerular cells, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, mesangial cells, fibroblasts, and infiltrating immune cells, placing this pathway at the intersection of inflammation, tissue injury, maladaptive repair, and chronic fibrotic remodeling.

Against this biological background, the interpretation of disease relevance should be framed cautiously because no direct publication set was supplied for this factor.

No relevant publications were provided in the input, and therefore no pathway-to-disease conclusion can be attributed to the supplied citation set. Nevertheless, based on established biological knowledge, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells is widely regarded as a major pathogenic regulator in kidney disease because it integrates many of the upstream stresses that characterize both acute and chronic renal injury, including ischemic stress, oxidative injury, metabolic dysregulation, protein overload, immune activation, and renin angiotensin signaling. In kidney tissue, activation of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells promotes transcription of proinflammatory cytokines, chemotactic mediators, adhesion molecules, and profibrotic effectors, thereby enhancing leukocyte infiltration, sustaining tubular and glomerular inflammation, and amplifying crosstalk among parenchymal cells and immune cells. Persistent activation of this transcriptional program contributes to podocyte injury, mesangial activation, tubular epithelial dysfunction, endothelial disturbance, and interstitial fibroblast activation, which together drive albumin leakage, decline in filtration capacity, and progressive scarring. This pathway is therefore mechanistically relevant across multiple forms of kidney disease, including diabetic kidney disease, immune-mediated glomerular injury, acute kidney injury, hypertensive nephropathy, and chronic kidney disease progression. Because the publication list is empty, these statements should be interpreted as a general pathway-based synthesis rather than a literature-grounded conclusion from the provided references.

Consistent with this pathway-centered interpretation, the enrichment results offer a quantitative basis for considering the potential relevance of this regulatory program to the analyzed kidney disease-associated protein set.

There were 44 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells, a central transcriptional regulatory program that integrates inflammatory, infectious, oxidative, metabolic, and hemodynamic stress signaling and directly controls target gene expression through the canonical deoxyribonucleic acid binding motif NGGGGAMTTTCCNN. This enrichment supports a strong functional connection between the analyzed protein set and kidney disease pathobiology, because nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling is active across multiple renal and inflammatory cell compartments, including glomerular cells, tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, mesangial cells, fibroblasts, and infiltrating immune cells, where it regulates cytokine production, chemokine expression, leukocyte recruitment, cell survival, adhesion, fibrosis, and innate immune activation. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 44 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive inspection.

To extend the interpretation of this 44-protein enrichment signal, the following paragraphs introduce several significant proteins in greater detail and consider how their annotated functions may relate to kidney disease mechanisms in a cautious and biologically reasoned manner.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

BST2 is highly relevant to kidney disease because interferon-driven innate immune activation, viral infection, and inflammatory tissue remodeling are recurrent themes in renal pathology. The kidney is frequently affected by systemic viral infections and by chronic interferon signaling, both of which can promote glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury. BST2 stands out as a host-defense molecule that directly restricts viral spread while simultaneously shaping inflammatory signaling. Its ability to activate NF-kappa-B, regulate plasmacytoid dendritic cell interferon responses, and influence epithelial cytoskeletal organization suggests that it could contribute not only to antiviral defense but also to maladaptive inflammation and epithelial stress within renal tissue. In addition, its inhibition of MMP14-associated proteolytic activity may be relevant to extracellular matrix turnover and migration, processes central to fibrosis and tissue remodeling in chronic kidney disease. Thus, BST2 is mechanistically interesting at the intersection of antiviral immunity, interferon biology, and renal inflammatory remodeling.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

From this interferon- and host-defense-oriented context, the next candidate further broadens the discussion toward injury adaptation, tissue remodeling, and immune cell polarization.

CHI3L1 is one of the strongest kidney disease-relevant candidates in this list because it integrates inflammation, tissue remodeling, epithelial stress responses, and macrophage polarization, all of which are central to acute and chronic renal injury. Kidney disease progression commonly involves tubular epithelial injury, inflammatory cell recruitment, maladaptive repair, and fibrogenic macrophage responses. CHI3L1 is functionally linked to these processes through its roles in regulating inflammatory cell apoptosis, dendritic cell accumulation, M2 macrophage differentiation, and tissue adaptation to injury. Its capacity to activate AKT1 signaling and induce IL8 also suggests a role in epithelial inflammatory amplification. These properties make CHI3L1 particularly relevant to tubulointerstitial inflammation and fibrosis, where persistent repair-associated signaling can drive chronic kidney disease progression. Even though the provided description emphasizes lung and intestinal contexts, the underlying biology—injury response, remodeling, and innate immune regulation—is highly transferable to renal disease mechanisms.

A related but distinct dimension of kidney disease biology involves vascular organization and endothelial stability, which makes the following protein especially noteworthy.

EPHB4 is especially important in the kidney because renal function depends on highly specialized vascular architecture and tightly regulated endothelial behavior. Glomerular filtration and peritubular capillary integrity are profoundly influenced by endothelial stability, vessel remodeling, and permeability control. The described functions of EPHB4 in angiogenesis, blood vessel remodeling, and permeability therefore have direct conceptual relevance to kidney disease, particularly diabetic kidney disease, ischemic injury, thrombotic microangiopathy, and progressive chronic kidney disease characterized by capillary rarefaction. Its role in controlling cell adhesion and migration also suggests involvement in endothelial-mesenchymal and stromal remodeling processes that accompany fibrosis. EPHB4 stands out as a vascular regulator with plausible importance in both glomerular and interstitial compartments of the diseased kidney.

This vascular theme continues in the next candidate, which is more specifically connected to endothelial junctional organization and barrier integrity.

ESAM is relevant to kidney disease because endothelial barrier integrity is essential for normal glomerular filtration and microvascular homeostasis. The kidney contains highly specialized endothelial beds, and disruption of endothelial junctions contributes to albuminuria, inflammation, edema, and progressive microvascular injury. By linking actin fibers to endothelial junctions, ESAM may influence vascular permeability and resistance to inflammatory or hemodynamic stress. This is particularly pertinent in glomerular diseases and systemic inflammatory states that damage the renal endothelium. Its role in endothelial cytoskeletal-junctional coupling also makes it relevant to capillary stability in chronic kidney disease, where endothelial dysfunction and capillary loss are major drivers of hypoxia and fibrosis.[PubMed:24806444](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24806444) 

Whereas the previous proteins emphasize vascular structure and barrier function, the next candidate shifts attention toward developmental and reparative signaling programs in renal tissue.

FGFR2 is highly pertinent to kidney biology because nephrogenesis and later repair programs depend on tightly coordinated growth factor signaling. The kidney develops through branching morphogenesis of the ureteric bud and reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signaling, processes conceptually aligned with the annotated FGFR2 functions. In disease, pathways that regulate proliferation, differentiation, and wound healing can become reactivated and contribute either to repair or to maladaptive fibrosis. Therefore, FGFR2 may be important in congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, as well as in post-injury epithelial regeneration and chronic fibrotic remodeling. It stands out because developmental regulators often have dual significance in both congenital renal disorders and acquired kidney disease progression.

This developmental perspective connects naturally to cytokine-responsive epithelial programs, which are also central to injury, repair, and chronic remodeling in the kidney.

IL22RA1 is notable in kidney disease because cytokine receptor signaling through JAK/STAT, MAPK, and Akt pathways is central to epithelial injury responses, inflammation, and tissue repair. In renal disease, tubular epithelial cells are major targets of cytokine-mediated stress and regeneration programs. The ability of IL22RA1-containing receptor complexes to transmit IL22-family signals suggests a plausible role in epithelial barrier protection or inflammatory activation, depending on context. Its connection to antiangiogenic signaling is also relevant, since microvascular rarefaction is a hallmark of chronic kidney disease progression. Accordingly, IL22RA1 stands out as a candidate linking epithelial cytokine responses with vascular remodeling, two processes that strongly influence renal outcome.

The focus then moves from epithelial signaling to immune amplification, an axis that is frequently decisive in both inflammatory kidney disease and transplant settings.

IL15RA is relevant to kidney disease because IL-15 signaling intersects with immune activation, leukocyte survival, and innate effector functions that can shape renal inflammation. The kidney is frequently infiltrated by neutrophils, macrophages, and lymphocytes in acute kidney injury, glomerulonephritis, and transplant rejection. IL15RA-mediated trans-presentation is particularly important for amplifying local immune responses, while its role in neutrophil SYK activation and phagocytosis suggests relevance to infection-associated renal injury and sterile inflammatory damage. Because renal disease often reflects a balance between protective host defense and harmful immune-mediated injury, IL15RA represents a meaningful immune-regulatory node with potential implications for both inflammatory nephropathies and transplant immunobiology.[PubMed:17947230](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17947230) 

A complementary immunoregulatory perspective is provided by the next protein, which may be more closely associated with immune restraint and inflammatory resolution.

LGALS1 is particularly interesting in kidney disease because immune cell survival, T-cell polarization, and inflammatory resolution are major determinants of renal injury and recovery. The protein's strong immunomodulatory profile—especially induction of T-cell apoptosis and suppression of Th17 differentiation—is directly relevant to autoimmune and inflammatory kidney disorders, including glomerulonephritis and transplant rejection. Th17-associated pathways are increasingly implicated in renal inflammation, and molecules that restrain this axis may influence disease severity. In addition, galectin-mediated effects on apoptosis and cell differentiation may affect resident renal cells during injury and fibrotic remodeling. Thus, LGALS1 stands out as a potentially protective immunoregulatory factor in the kidney, although its effects may vary with disease context and cell type.[PubMed:24752896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24752896) 

In parallel with immune regulation, inflammatory vascular remodeling remains another important component of renal pathobiology, which makes the next candidate conceptually relevant.

Although the annotation is concise, TNFAIP2 is relevant because inflammation and angiogenesis are both central to kidney disease pathogenesis. Inflammatory cytokine-driven endothelial activation and abnormal vascular remodeling contribute to glomerular injury, interstitial hypoxia, and fibrosis. A protein induced in inflammatory settings and linked to angiogenesis may therefore participate in renal endothelial responses, leukocyte recruitment, and remodeling of the microvasculature. TNFAIP2 stands out as a plausible mediator of the inflammatory-vascular interface that is especially important in chronic kidney disease and inflammatory nephropathies.

This interface between inflammation and tissue infiltration is developed further by the following protein, which may influence leukocyte entry into injured renal compartments.

ADAM8 is relevant to kidney disease because leukocyte recruitment into renal tissue is a core mechanism in acute and chronic inflammatory nephropathies. Extravasation of circulating immune cells into the glomerulus or interstitium contributes to tissue injury, cytokine amplification, and subsequent fibrosis. A molecule implicated in leukocyte trafficking may therefore influence the severity of nephritic inflammation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, and allograft rejection. ADAM8 stands out as a candidate connecting protease activity with inflammatory cell infiltration, a process that often determines renal damage progression.

In contrast, the next protein may be more relevant as an endogenous inhibitory signal that tempers excessive innate immune activation in the kidney.

CD300A is of interest in kidney disease because excessive innate immune activation is a major driver of renal injury. TLR-MYD88 signaling contributes to sterile inflammation in acute kidney injury, autoimmune nephritis, and chronic kidney disease. By negatively regulating this pathway, CD300A may function as an endogenous brake on inflammatory amplification. Its inhibitory effects on NK cells and mast cells further support relevance to transplant rejection, immune-mediated glomerular disease, and allergic or inflammatory renal injury. Thus, CD300A stands out as a potentially protective immunoregulatory receptor in the renal inflammatory environment.[PubMed:12874256](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12874256) [PubMed:12893283](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12893283) [PubMed:16339535](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16339535) 

Another immune-associated candidate in this set may act through macrophage state regulation, thereby influencing whether renal injury resolves or progresses.

DPEP2 is potentially important in kidney disease because macrophages are central orchestrators of renal injury, repair, and fibrosis. The transition between inflammatory and reparative macrophage states strongly influences whether the kidney recovers or progresses to chronic disease. A protein that regulates macrophage NF-kappaB signaling could therefore affect cytokine production, tubular injury, and fibrotic remodeling. DPEP2 stands out because it may have noncanonical signaling functions beyond metabolism, making it a plausible modulator of the inflammatory microenvironment in tubulointerstitial disease.

Beyond inflammatory control, kidney disease also reflects disruption of core physiological transport functions, which provides context for the next protein.

CA4 is relevant to kidney disease because acid-base homeostasis is one of the kidney's most fundamental physiological roles. Proteins that regulate bicarbonate handling and intracellular pH are directly linked to tubular transport function, systemic acid-base balance, and susceptibility to tubular stress. Disturbance of bicarbonate transport contributes to renal tubular acidosis, metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease, and altered epithelial cell viability under injurious conditions. CA4 therefore stands out as a transporter-related candidate with direct physiological relevance to renal tubular function and disease.

The next candidate is less directly tied to canonical renal physiology, yet it may still be relevant through effects on epithelial regeneration after injury.

CTSS is a more indirect but still potentially relevant kidney disease candidate because control of cell-cycle progression is critical in renal epithelial regeneration after injury. Following acute kidney injury, surviving tubular cells re-enter the cell cycle, and dysregulated mitosis can promote maladaptive repair, polyploidy, senescence, or fibrosis. A molecule implicated in mitotic progression may therefore influence the quality of epithelial repair. Although the provided annotation is limited and not kidney-specific, CTSS remains of interest in the broader context of renal injury and regeneration biology.

From epithelial repair, the discussion returns to adaptive immunity, particularly pathways that may shape cytotoxic lymphocyte-mediated renal injury.

TNFRSF9 is relevant to kidney disease because cytotoxic T-cell activation is a major determinant of renal allograft rejection, virus-associated renal injury, and some forms of immune-mediated nephritis. By strengthening CD8-positive T-cell survival and effector function, TNFRSF9 signaling could amplify tissue-directed immune injury in the kidney, particularly in transplantation and chronic viral infection. At the same time, this pathway may be beneficial in antiviral defense. Its importance lies in the fact that renal pathology often emerges from the same immune circuits that are protective in infection but damaging when excessive or misdirected.

A closely related but mechanistically distinct process in renal injury is programmed cell death, which is highlighted by the following receptor.

TNFRSF10B is mechanistically relevant to kidney disease because apoptosis of tubular epithelial cells, endothelial cells, and immune cells is a major feature of both acute and chronic renal injury. TRAIL pathway signaling can influence whether stressed renal cells undergo death or survive, thereby affecting inflammation, tubular atrophy, and fibrosis. The balance between death-inducing receptors and decoy receptors is especially important in determining tissue outcome under inflammatory conditions. TNFRSF10B therefore stands out as a plausible mediator of renal cell loss and injury progression.[PubMed:10549288](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10549288) [PubMed:26457518](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26457518) 

Finally, the list concludes with a broader transcriptional regulator whose relevance may emerge through immune control and cell survival pathways upstream of overt renal injury phenotypes.

ZBTB17 is relevant to kidney disease primarily through immune regulation and cell survival. Adaptive immune responses are central to autoimmune nephritis and transplant rejection, and transcriptional regulators that control lymphocyte development and apoptosis can shape the composition and persistence of pathogenic immune populations. In addition, its broader role in cell-cycle regulation suggests possible relevance to injury responses in renal resident cells. ZBTB17 stands out as an upstream regulatory factor whose effects may be less kidney-specific but potentially significant in immune-mediated renal disease.

### Colon; endocrine cells[≥Medium] (HPA:0131292) 

Colon endocrine cells are specialized epithelial cells dispersed within the colonic mucosa that sense luminal nutrients, microbial metabolites, bile acid derivatives, inflammatory signals, and mechanical stimuli, and translate these inputs into hormonal and paracrine outputs. These cells include several functionally distinct populations that produce mediators such as serotonin, glucagon-like peptide one, glucagon-like peptide two, peptide tyrosine tyrosine, neurotensin, somatostatin, and other bioactive factors. Through these secretory products, colon endocrine cells regulate intestinal motility, epithelial barrier integrity, mucosal immune tone, nutrient handling, visceral sensory signaling, and communication with distant organs through neural, endocrine, and metabolic routes. In a broader physiological context, this pathway represents the endocrine interface of the colon within the gut-kidney axis, whereby changes in microbial ecology, fermentation products, epithelial health, and intestinal inflammation can alter endocrine cell activity and thereby influence systemic metabolism, vascular function, immune activation, and toxin handling. Because kidney disease is strongly shaped by chronic inflammation, metabolic dysregulation, vascular injury, and accumulation of gut-derived uremic solutes, the biological functions of colon endocrine cells are conceptually relevant to kidney pathophysiology even when direct pathway-specific evidence is limited.

With this physiological background in mind, the currently available evidence should be interpreted cautiously. No relevant publications were provided for this pathway, so a direct literature-based linkage between colon endocrine cells and kidney disease cannot be established from the supplied evidence. Nevertheless, from a biological perspective, colon endocrine cells are plausibly connected to kidney disease through the gut-kidney axis. In kidney dysfunction, alterations in intestinal transit, microbial composition, mucosal permeability, and luminal metabolite profiles are common, and these disturbances are expected to modify endocrine cell stimulation and secretory behavior in the colon. Such changes may influence systemic inflammatory tone, glucose and energy homeostasis, vascular regulation, appetite, and epithelial barrier maintenance, all of which are processes that affect the initiation or progression of kidney injury. In addition, colon endocrine signaling may indirectly shape the generation or absorption of gut-derived metabolites that accumulate when renal clearance declines, thereby contributing to the systemic complications of kidney disease. However, because no supporting publications were supplied, this relationship should be regarded as a mechanistic and hypothesis-generating interpretation rather than a conclusion supported by the provided citation set.

Although the direct literature support is limited, the enrichment results provide a quantitative basis for considering this pathway further. There were 55 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing colon endocrine cells as specialized epithelial cells distributed within the colonic mucosa that detect luminal nutrients, microbial metabolites, bile acid derivatives, inflammatory signals, and mechanical stimuli, and convert these inputs into hormonal and paracrine outputs. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway integrates multiple processes that are highly relevant to kidney disease pathophysiology, including regulation of intestinal motility, epithelial barrier integrity, mucosal immune tone, nutrient handling, visceral sensory signaling, and communication with distant organs through neural, endocrine, and metabolic routes. In the context of kidney disease, the functional relevance is strengthened by the fact that chronic inflammation, metabolic dysregulation, vascular injury, and retention of gut-derived uremic solutes are all major disease features, and each of these processes can be influenced by altered colon endocrine cell activity within the gut-kidney axis. Thus, the identification of 55 enriched proteins supports a quantitatively substantial connection between this intestinal endocrine pathway and kidney disease biology.
