Building on this network-level overview, the following section summarizes the proteins that appeared particularly significant in the functional enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

NOTCH1 stands out as one of the most kidney-relevant proteins in this list because Notch signaling is a central regulator of renal development, tubular epithelial differentiation, and glomerular homeostasis. The annotated functions indicate broad control over differentiation, proliferation, apoptosis, and angiogenesis, all of which are core processes in kidney injury and repair. In kidney disease, aberrant reactivation of Notch signaling has been strongly linked to tubulointerstitial fibrosis, podocyte injury, and maladaptive epithelial repair. Its role in endothelial biology is also highly relevant because microvascular rarefaction and endothelial dysfunction are major drivers of chronic kidney disease progression. Thus, the known developmental and angiogenic functions of NOTCH1 provide a mechanistic framework for its likely contribution to renal fibrosis, epithelial plasticity, and capillary remodeling.

In a related vascular and matrix-remodeling context, COL18A1 also appears potentially important. COL18A1 is highly relevant to kidney disease because the renal microvasculature is essential for filtration, oxygen delivery, and maintenance of tubulointerstitial integrity. The anti-angiogenic properties of COL18A1, particularly its ability to inhibit vascular endothelial growth factor A-driven endothelial proliferation and migration, are notable in the context of glomerular and peritubular capillary biology. Vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling is indispensable for glomerular endothelial health, and dysregulation of this pathway contributes to proteinuria, endothelial injury, and chronic kidney disease progression. Therefore, COL18A1 may influence kidney disease through modulation of endothelial survival, capillary remodeling, and extracellular matrix-endothelial interactions. Its integrin-related effects further suggest a role in matrix remodeling, a hallmark of renal fibrosis.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

Shifting from vascular regulation to inflammatory injury, IL18 emerges as another strong candidate. IL18 is one of the most compelling kidney disease candidates in the list because it directly links inflammation, epithelial injury, and pyroptotic cell death. These processes are central to both acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease. The annotation emphasizes its role in epithelial barrier repair and inflammatory signaling, which is highly pertinent to renal tubular epithelium, where sterile inflammation and inflammasome activation are major pathogenic mechanisms. IL18 has been widely studied as a biomarker and mediator of tubular injury, especially in ischemic and inflammatory kidney damage. Its release downstream of pyroptosis is particularly important because inflammasome-driven tubular and immune-cell injury contributes to disease amplification, fibrosis, and loss of renal function.[PubMed:26638072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638072) [PubMed:26638073](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638073) [PubMed:30392956](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30392956) 

Consistent with this inflammatory theme, LGALS3 may also be relevant to progressive renal injury. LGALS3 is particularly important in kidney disease because it integrates inflammation, tissue remodeling, and cellular stress responses. Galectin-3 has been strongly implicated in renal fibrosis, macrophage recruitment, and progression of chronic kidney disease. The listed functions support this interpretation: it promotes inflammatory cell activation and chemoattraction, influences endothelial migration, and participates in damage sensing and autophagy-related pathways. In the kidney, these activities could contribute to sustained interstitial inflammation, defective resolution of injury, and fibrotic remodeling. Because chronic kidney disease progression depends heavily on inflammatory-fibrotic crosstalk, LGALS3 represents a biologically plausible mediator and biomarker of adverse renal outcomes.

Another immune regulatory protein of possible interest is SIRPA. SIRPA is relevant to kidney disease because the cluster of differentiation forty-seven-signal regulatory protein alpha axis is increasingly recognized as a regulator of inflammation, phagocytic clearance, and tissue injury responses. In the kidney, impaired clearance of apoptotic cells and persistent innate immune activation can exacerbate both acute and chronic injury. The documented ability of SIRPA to suppress phagocytosis and modulate dendritic-cell activation suggests a role in controlling renal immune homeostasis, while its involvement in reactive oxygen species signaling is important because oxidative stress is a major component of ischemic, diabetic, and inflammatory nephropathies. These functions make SIRPA mechanistically interesting in the context of renal inflammation, maladaptive repair, and fibrosis.[PubMed:18045614](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18045614) [PubMed:30726215](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30726215) 

Beyond inflammatory signaling, several proteins point toward mitochondrial vulnerability in kidney disease. CHCHD10 is notable because mitochondrial integrity is fundamental to kidney function, especially in energetically demanding tubular epithelial cells. The maintenance of mitochondrial organization and cristae structure is directly relevant to renal pathophysiology, as mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to acute tubular injury, oxidative stress, defective fatty acid oxidation, and chronic fibrotic remodeling. Although the annotation is concise, proteins that preserve cristae architecture are often critical determinants of cellular survival under hypoxic or toxic stress. In kidney disease, disruption of mitochondrial ultrastructure can impair adenosine triphosphate production and trigger apoptosis or inflammatory signaling, making CHCHD10 a plausible contributor to tubular vulnerability.

Closely aligned with this mitochondrial theme, BNIP3L may also influence renal epithelial fate under stress. BNIP3L is highly relevant to kidney disease because apoptosis and mitochondrial quality control are central determinants of renal epithelial survival during stress. Tubular cells are exceptionally sensitive to hypoxia, ischemia, and metabolic injury, all of which damage mitochondria. The annotated role of BNIP3L in mitochondrial protein catabolism and removal of damage links it to mitophagy-like quality control pathways that can either protect cells or, when dysregulated, promote cell death. In kidney disorders such as ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic kidney disease, and chronic hypoxic nephropathy, imbalance between mitochondrial repair and apoptosis is a key pathogenic mechanism. BNIP3L therefore stands out as a protein that may influence whether injured renal cells recover or undergo degeneration.

In addition to mitochondrial quality control, lysosomal proteostasis appears repeatedly among the enriched proteins. CTSD is relevant to kidney disease because lysosomal proteolysis is essential for proximal tubular protein handling, autophagic flux, and degradation of damaged intracellular components. Although the annotation does not explicitly mention renal biology, cathepsin D is a major lysosomal protease, and lysosomal dysfunction is increasingly recognized in proteinuric kidney disease, tubular injury, and age-related renal decline. In the kidney, defective degradation pathways can promote accumulation of damaged proteins, inflammation, and cell death. Thus, CTSD likely has mechanistic importance in maintaining renal proteostasis, particularly in tubular epithelial cells exposed to high endocytic and metabolic stress.[PubMed:27333034](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27333034) 

A similar interpretation may apply to CTSH. CTSH merits attention because lysosomal protein degradation is a fundamental process in renal tubular cells, which continuously reabsorb and process filtered proteins. Disturbance of lysosomal function contributes to tubular toxicity, defective autophagy, inflammation, and progressive chronic kidney disease. Given the centrality of lysosomal proteostasis in the kidney, CTSH may be relevant to disorders characterized by protein overload, tubular stress, or impaired intracellular clearance. Even though the annotation is brief, the function itself is highly pertinent to renal pathobiology.

Metabolic stress is another major axis represented in this protein set. FABP1 is strongly connected to kidney disease through lipid metabolism and lipotoxicity. Abnormal intracellular lipid handling is increasingly recognized as a driver of tubular injury, oxidative stress, and fibrosis in diabetic kidney disease and obesity-associated nephropathy. The ability of FABP1 to bind fatty acids and cholesterol and mediate intracellular lipid transport is therefore highly relevant to renal metabolic stress. Although FABP1 is classically associated with liver biology, urinary fatty acid binding protein family proteins have also been explored as markers of tubular injury. Mechanistically, dysregulated lipid trafficking in renal epithelial cells can trigger inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and progressive nephron loss, making FABP1 a biologically meaningful candidate.

From metabolic regulation, the discussion can be extended to cyclic nucleotide signaling and epithelial homeostasis. GUCA2A is potentially relevant to kidney disease because guanylate cyclase-cyclic guanosine monophosphate signaling has important effects on epithelial transport, vascular tone, and fluid-electrolyte balance. While the annotation emphasizes intestinal biology, this signaling axis is conceptually linked to cardiorenal and salt-handling pathways. Molecules that modulate cyclic nucleotide signaling may influence renal hemodynamics or epithelial transport indirectly, and gut-derived endocrine factors are increasingly appreciated as contributors to systemic metabolic and inflammatory states that affect the kidney. Accordingly, GUCA2A is not among the strongest candidates here, but it remains mechanistically interesting in a broader epithelial and fluid homeostasis context.

A similarly indirect but potentially informative endocrine candidate is INSL5. INSL5 is a more indirect but still potentially relevant candidate because endocrine and metabolic signaling pathways often shape kidney disease susceptibility. Although its annotated functions are centered on gut and thymic biology, peptide hormones acting through G-protein-coupled receptors can influence systemic metabolism, appetite, and inflammatory tone, all of which are important modifiers of chronic kidney disease risk. At present, the kidney connection is less direct than for inflammatory, angiogenic, or mitochondrial proteins in this list, but INSL5 may warrant consideration in the context of gut-kidney endocrine communication.

The enrichment set also includes proteins that may connect mucosal immunity to renal disease. PIGR is relevant to kidney disease because immunoglobulin A biology is central to immunoglobulin A nephropathy, one of the most common primary glomerular diseases worldwide. Although PIGR primarily functions in mucosal immunity and epithelial transport of polymeric immunoglobulins, abnormalities in mucosal immunoglobulin A handling, production, and glycosylation are deeply implicated in the pathogenesis of immunoglobulin A nephropathy. Therefore, proteins involved in polymeric immunoglobulin A biology may have indirect but meaningful links to renal disease susceptibility and immune complex formation. PIGR is especially interesting from the perspective of the gut-mucosa-kidney axis.

In contrast to these indirect immune links, PTPRN2 has a more explicit connection to renal regulatory systems. PTPRN2 is one of the most kidney-relevant proteins in the list because it is explicitly required to maintain normal renin expression and renin release, directly connecting it to the renin-angiotensin system, a master regulator of renal hemodynamics, sodium balance, and chronic kidney disease progression. Its role in insulin secretion also adds relevance because diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease. Furthermore, its phosphoinositide phosphatase activity and effects on actin dynamics suggest broader influence on secretory cell function and possibly glomerular or tubular cellular architecture. Taken together, PTPRN2 may intersect kidney disease through endocrine regulation, blood pressure control, and diabetes-related mechanisms.[PubMed:21732083](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21732083) [PubMed:15220191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220191) [PubMed:16418280](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16418280) [PubMed:16269463](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16269463) [PubMed:19019914](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19019914) [PubMed:12364328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12364328) 

Developmental and epithelial repair programs are also represented in the enriched set. SOX9 is highly relevant to kidney disease because it is explicitly involved in epithelial branching during kidney development and more broadly regulates epithelial progenitor behavior. Developmental transcription factors often re-emerge during renal injury, where they can mark regenerative responses or maladaptive epithelial plasticity. In the kidney, SOX9-positive epithelial cells have been associated with repair programs after injury, and persistent activation of developmental pathways can influence fibrosis and tubular remodeling. Thus, the annotated developmental and epithelial functions of SOX9 support a meaningful connection to congenital renal anomalies, injury-repair responses, and chronic remodeling.[PubMed:24038782](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24038782) [PubMed:8640233](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8640233) 

Some additional proteins may be of interest, although the available evidence is more limited. Although no function is annotated here, CA12 may still be of interest in kidney disease because carbonic anhydrases are generally involved in acid-base regulation, bicarbonate handling, and epithelial ion transport, which are core renal functions. However, without a supplied functional description or citation in the present dataset, its kidney relevance cannot be confidently prioritized relative to stronger candidates such as NOTCH1, IL18, COL18A1, PTPRN2, or SOX9.

Finally, LGALS4 may have a moderate connection to kidney disease through epithelial barrier organization and cell-cell adhesion. Adherens junction integrity is important in renal tubular epithelia, where loss of epithelial cohesion contributes to injury and dedifferentiation. However, compared with LGALS3, the evidence provided here is less directly linked to inflammation or fibrosis, so LGALS4 is best considered a secondary candidate with possible relevance to epithelial structural maintenance.

### Duodenum; enterocytes[≥Medium] (HPA:0151302) 

The pathway label indicates molecular activity detected in enterocytes of the duodenum at at least medium abundance. Enterocytes are the principal absorptive epithelial cells of the proximal small intestine and are central to the uptake, intracellular processing, and transepithelial transport of nutrients, minerals, lipids, peptides, xenobiotics, and many orally administered drugs. In the duodenum, these cells are also major regulators of iron handling, calcium absorption, phosphate sensing, bile acid exposure responses, and communication with the gut microbiota and immune system. Because the duodenum is the first segment of the small intestine to receive gastric contents, pancreatic enzymes, and bile, enterocyte pathways in this region are especially important for nutrient sensing and for endocrine signaling to distant organs. From a pathophysiological perspective, duodenal enterocyte programs can influence systemic metabolic homeostasis, inflammation, uremic toxin generation, barrier integrity, and mineral balance, all of which are highly relevant to kidney disease. However, the present pathway description is nonspecific and does not identify a defined molecular cascade, transporter system, signaling module, or gene set beyond its anatomical and cellular localization.

Given this limited definition, the interpretation of disease relevance must remain cautious and closely tied to the information actually provided. No relevant publications were provided, and the pathway description itself is limited to tissue and cell type localization rather than a defined biological mechanism. Therefore, a direct evidence-based linkage between this pathway and kidney disease cannot be established from the supplied material. In general, duodenal enterocyte biology can be related to kidney disease through several well-recognized physiological axes, including regulation of mineral metabolism, intestinal barrier function, systemic inflammation, and handling of dietary compounds that may alter the burden of solutes normally excreted by the kidney. Disturbance of intestinal epithelial transport and signaling may contribute to chronic kidney disease by modifying calcium, phosphate, and iron homeostasis, and by influencing generation or absorption of gut-derived metabolites that accumulate when renal clearance declines. Conversely, kidney disease can alter the intestinal environment and enterocyte function through uremia, inflammation, and changes in the microbiome. Nevertheless, because no publications were supplied and no specific enterocyte pathway was defined, any stronger claim about causality, mechanism, or clinical significance would be speculative and unsupported by the provided evidence.

Although the mechanistic annotation remains broad, the enrichment result still provides a quantitative basis for considering possible biological relevance. There were 58 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway described as molecular activity detected in enterocytes of the duodenum at at least medium abundance. This protein set size of 58 supports a biologically substantive enrichment signal and is notable in the context of kidney disease because duodenal enterocytes are quantitatively central to nutrient absorption, mineral handling, xenobiotic processing, endocrine communication, and barrier regulation, each of which can influence systemic processes relevant to renal pathophysiology, including inflammation, metabolic homeostasis, uremic solute burden, and mineral imbalance. Although the pathway label does not define a single molecular cascade, signaling axis, or transporter program, the enrichment of 58 proteins indicates a measurable convergence between kidney disease-associated proteins and epithelial functions localized to the proximal small intestine, particularly in the first intestinal segment exposed to gastric contents, bile, and pancreatic enzymes.

To place this enrichment in a network context, the interaction map is shown below together with the corresponding external resource for direct inspection. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network for these 58 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct interactive inspection of network connectivity and functional relationships.

![PPI Network](imgs/04c4b2b3-df27-4f4c-ae59-a5b0c599bfa4.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=D0353C91FE3CAF4C)

With this broader context in mind, the following paragraphs introduce several of the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and discuss their possible relevance to kidney biology in a careful, evidence-aware manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

NOTCH1 stands out as one of the most kidney-relevant proteins in this list because Notch signaling is a well-established regulator of nephrogenesis, tubular epithelial cell fate, and renal injury responses. The annotated function indicates broad control over differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis, all of which are central processes in chronic kidney disease, tubular repair, and renal fibrosis. In the kidney, aberrant reactivation of developmental pathways such as NOTCH1 in mature tubular epithelium has been linked to maladaptive repair, epithelial dedifferentiation, and profibrotic signaling. Its role in angiogenesis is also pertinent, because microvascular rarefaction is a key feature of progressive chronic kidney disease. In addition, the note that NOTCH1 is involved in epithelial differentiation and branching programs is highly relevant to renal development, as nephron segmentation and collecting system morphogenesis depend on tightly regulated developmental signaling. Overall, NOTCH1 is important because it connects developmental biology with injury-induced remodeling, two major axes of kidney disease pathogenesis.

In a similarly epithelial context, PDZK1 appears notable because its annotated function points directly to transport-related organization in renal tubular cells. Among the listed proteins, PDZK1 has one of the most direct links to renal physiology because its annotated activity explicitly involves the proximal tubule. The proximal tubule depends on polarized apical trafficking of transporters for solute reclamation, acid-base regulation, and phosphate handling. PDZK1 functions as a scaffold that stabilizes membrane protein complexes in epithelial brush border domains, thereby influencing transporter localization and activity. Disruption of this type of scaffolding can impair tubular transport, alter phosphate balance, and contribute to nephrolithiasis or chronic kidney disease-associated mineral metabolism disorders. Its role in SCARB1-mediated cholesterol handling further suggests a connection to renal lipid stress. Collectively, these functions make PDZK1 a particularly compelling kidney-related protein in this dataset.

Moving from epithelial transport to inflammatory signaling, IL18 provides a clearer link to injury-associated immune activation. IL18 is highly relevant to kidney disease because it is a major mediator of sterile inflammation, inflammasome activation, and epithelial injury, all of which are central to acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease progression. The annotation explicitly connects IL18 to pyroptosis and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells-driven inflammatory cascades, mechanisms that are increasingly recognized in ischemic, toxic, and inflammatory renal damage. In renal tubular epithelial cells, inflammasome activation can amplify leukocyte recruitment, endothelial dysfunction, and fibrogenic remodeling. The stated role in epithelial barrier repair is also pertinent because tubular epithelial integrity is a key determinant of renal recovery after injury. Therefore, IL18 stands out as both a mechanistic biomarker and a potential effector of kidney injury, particularly in settings characterized by innate immune activation and cell death-associated inflammation.[PubMed:26638072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638072) [PubMed:26638073](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26638073) [PubMed:30392956](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30392956) 

Closely related to this inflammatory theme, GCHFR may be relevant because its annotation also converges on inflammasome regulation. GCHFR is notable in the kidney disease context because it is directly linked to inflammasome biology, specifically non-canonical NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 activation. NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 inflammasome signaling has been strongly implicated in acute kidney injury, diabetic kidney disease, crystal nephropathy, and progressive interstitial fibrosis. The annotation suggests that GCHFR functions as a sensor integrating microbial products and mitochondrial danger-associated molecular patterns, thereby amplifying inflammatory signaling. This is especially relevant in the kidney, where tubular injury and mitochondrial dysfunction release endogenous danger signals that can perpetuate sterile inflammation. By promoting the interaction of NLR family pyrin domain containing 3 with never in mitosis gene A-related kinase 7, GCHFR may help drive a feed-forward inflammatory response that worsens tissue injury and impairs repair. For this reason, GCHFR represents an interesting upstream regulator of innate immune activation with plausible importance in inflammatory renal disease.

Another protein that fits within this inflammatory and stress-response framework is LGALS3, which has broad links to tissue remodeling. LGALS3 (galectin-3) is one of the strongest candidates for kidney relevance because it integrates inflammation, macrophage biology, epithelial stress responses, and damage-associated autophagy. These processes are central to both acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease. The annotation emphasizes leukocyte recruitment and activation, which are critical drivers of tubulointerstitial inflammation and fibrosis. Its role in recognizing membrane damage and mobilizing autophagy machinery is also important, since defective stress adaptation in tubular cells contributes to maladaptive repair. In renal disease, galectin-3 has been widely associated with fibrosis, macrophage accumulation, and adverse remodeling. Thus, the listed functions support a biologically coherent connection between LGALS3 and progressive kidney injury, particularly through inflammatory and profibrotic pathways.

Shifting from injury signaling to developmental control, SOX9 introduces a complementary perspective on kidney formation and repair. SOX9 is highly relevant because the annotation explicitly states that it controls epithelial branching during kidney development. This makes it important for nephrogenesis and congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract. In addition, SOX9 is increasingly recognized as a marker of injured and regenerative tubular epithelial states in adult kidneys. Its general functions in progenitor regulation, differentiation, and extracellular matrix control suggest that it may influence how renal epithelial cells respond to injury, either toward adaptive repair or fibrotic remodeling. Consequently, SOX9 stands out as a developmental regulator with likely importance in both congenital and acquired kidney disorders.[PubMed:24038782](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24038782) [PubMed:8640233](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8640233) 

At the level of organelle homeostasis, CHCHD10 may also be relevant because renal tubular function is strongly dependent on mitochondrial integrity. CHCHD10 is relevant to kidney disease because mitochondrial integrity is essential for renal tubular function, especially in energy-demanding nephron segments such as the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb. The annotation links CHCHD10 to mitochondrial organization and cristae maintenance, processes that directly affect oxidative phosphorylation, reactive oxygen species generation, and susceptibility to cell death. Mitochondrial structural failure is a common feature of ischemic injury, toxic nephropathy, and chronic kidney disease progression. Therefore, although the listed function is concise, CHCHD10 stands out mechanistically as a candidate contributor to renal vulnerability through impaired mitochondrial homeostasis.

Consistent with this mitochondrial theme, BNIP3L may contribute at the interface between organelle quality control and cell survival. BNIP3L is important in the context of kidney disease because it links apoptosis with mitochondrial quality control, two processes that strongly influence tubular cell survival after injury. Renal tubular cells are highly dependent on mitochondrial health, and failure to clear damaged mitochondria can promote oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis. The annotation indicates that BNIP3L participates in mitochondrial damage responses and can induce apoptosis, suggesting a dual role in either adaptation or cell loss depending on context. Such mechanisms are highly relevant to acute kidney injury, where mitochondrial injury is an early event, and to chronic kidney disease, where persistent mitochondrial dysfunction contributes to progressive nephron loss. BNIP3L therefore stands out as a plausible modulator of renal epithelial fate under stress.

Beyond epithelial and mitochondrial responses, vascular regulation is another major axis of kidney disease, which brings COL18A1 into focus. COL18A1 is relevant to kidney disease because endothelial homeostasis and angiogenic signaling are central determinants of glomerular and peritubular capillary integrity. The kidney is highly vascularized, and progressive loss of microvasculature contributes to chronic hypoxia, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and chronic kidney disease progression. The annotation indicates that COL18A1 has anti-angiogenic activity and can antagonize vascular endothelial growth factor A signaling, a pathway with critical roles in glomerular endothelial maintenance. Dysregulation of this balance may contribute to endothelial dysfunction, capillary dropout, or altered repair responses after injury. Thus, COL18A1 is notable as a matrix-derived regulator of vascular biology with plausible implications for renal microvascular disease.[PubMed:9459295](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9459295) [PubMed:11257123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11257123) 

A related but more metabolic dimension is represented by FABP1, which may connect this protein set to lipid-associated renal stress. FABP1 is potentially important for kidney disease because lipid handling is increasingly recognized as a determinant of tubular injury and metabolic stress. Although FABP1 is classically associated with hepatocytes, its annotated role in intracellular lipid transport and cholesterol binding is relevant to renal lipotoxicity, particularly in diabetic kidney disease and proteinuric states where fatty acid overload can damage tubular epithelial cells. Abnormal intracellular lipid accumulation promotes oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory signaling in the kidney. Therefore, FABP1 stands out as a metabolically relevant protein whose function aligns with recognized mechanisms of renal injury.

At the level of intracellular stress adaptation, TXNDC5 may be pertinent because protein folding capacity is increasingly recognized as a determinant of renal cell resilience. TXNDC5 is relevant to kidney disease because endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis and oxidative protein folding are important determinants of renal cell survival under metabolic and inflammatory stress. The annotation identifies TXNDC5 as a protein disulfide isomerase, implicating it in endoplasmic reticulum stress responses. Endoplasmic reticulum stress is a major contributor to diabetic kidney disease, podocyte injury, and tubular epithelial dysfunction. By influencing protein folding capacity and redox balance, TXNDC5 may affect how renal cells cope with high secretory demand, oxidative injury, and chronic metabolic stress. This makes TXNDC5 a biologically plausible contributor to kidney pathology, particularly in diseases characterized by maladaptive unfolded protein responses.[PubMed:12930873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12930873) [PubMed:14971039](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971039) 

Finally, RBP2 provides a more indirect but still potentially meaningful connection through retinoid handling and epithelial differentiation. RBP2 is of potential interest for kidney disease because retinoid signaling has important effects on epithelial differentiation, repair, and metabolic regulation. Although the annotation is brief, intracellular retinol transport can influence local availability of retinoic acid, a pathway implicated in podocyte biology, tubular regeneration, and anti-fibrotic responses. Because the kidney participates in vitamin A metabolism and is responsive to retinoid signaling, proteins that regulate intracellular retinol trafficking may affect susceptibility to injury or repair capacity. Thus, RBP2 may have a more indirect but still meaningful connection to renal pathophysiology.

### actin-based cell projection (GO:0098858) 

Actin-based cell projections are membrane extensions whose structural core is formed by polymerized actin filaments rather than microtubules. This category includes diverse protrusive structures that support cell shape, environmental sensing, adhesion, migration, endocytosis, and specialized intercellular interactions. Their formation depends on tightly regulated actin nucleation, elongation, bundling, branching, and anchoring to membrane-associated protein complexes. In epithelial and endothelial tissues, actin-based projections help organize the cell surface and maintain barrier properties. In the kidney, the most biologically important example is the podocyte foot process, a highly specialized actin-rich projection that interdigitates with neighboring foot processes to form the slit diaphragm, a key component of the glomerular filtration barrier. The integrity of these projections requires continuous remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton in response to mechanical force, extracellular matrix attachment, and signaling from slit diaphragm proteins. Disturbance of actin filament organization within these projections can lead to foot process effacement, loss of filtration selectivity, protein leakage into the urine, and progressive glomerular injury. Thus, the pathway of actin-based cell projection formation and maintenance appears central to renal cellular architecture and filtration function.

Building on this structural framework, the disease relevance of this pathway can be considered in the context of established renal cell biology. Although no pathway-specific publications were provided, the relationship between actin-based cell projections and kidney disease is strongly supported by established renal cell biology. In the kidney, podocytes rely on elaborate actin-based foot processes to preserve the glomerular filtration barrier, and disease states commonly disrupt these projections through actin cytoskeletal disorganization. When signaling pathways that regulate actin assembly, membrane linkage, or adhesion to the glomerular basement membrane are impaired, podocyte foot processes retract and broaden, a structural change known as effacement, which is a hallmark of many proteinuric kidney diseases including minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, diabetic kidney disease, and other glomerulopathies. Because these projections are essential for maintaining slit diaphragm architecture and biomechanical resilience, their injury directly contributes to albuminuria and progressive loss of kidney function. Beyond podocytes, actin-based projections in tubular epithelial and immune cells may also influence epithelial repair, cell migration, and inflammatory responses in diseased kidneys. Therefore, this pathway may be best understood as a core structural and regulatory program whose disruption could undermine renal filtration barrier integrity and promote the initiation and progression of kidney disease.

This biological interpretation is further supported by the enrichment results obtained in the present analysis. There were 17 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing actin-based cell projections as membrane extensions supported by polymerized actin filaments rather than microtubules. This enrichment is highly relevant to renal biology because actin-based projections are essential for epithelial and endothelial surface organization, and in the kidney they are especially critical for podocyte foot processes, which form the slit diaphragm and preserve the glomerular filtration barrier. Given that this pathway centers on actin nucleation, elongation, bundling, branching, and membrane anchoring, the identification of 17 proteins indicates a substantial disease-associated signal connecting cytoskeletal remodeling to filtration barrier stability, mechanical stress adaptation, extracellular matrix attachment, and progressive glomerular injury. Disturbance of these actin-rich projections is directly consistent with key pathological features of kidney disease, including foot process effacement, reduced filtration selectivity, and protein leakage into the urine. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 17 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

[![PPI Network](imgs/d6ab139e-4ad3-40af-9825-852898a6eccb.png)](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=74690347379BE9A5)
[Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=74690347379BE9A5)

To further connect the enrichment signal with plausible disease mechanisms, the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis are discussed below in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

CBLIF is the most directly relevant protein in this list for kidney disease because its annotated function explicitly places it in the renal proximal tubule, where receptor-mediated endocytosis is essential for reclamation of filtered proteins and micronutrients. Its ability to bind albumin, transferrin, hemoglobin, high-density lipoprotein-related ligands, and vitamin carriers strongly connects it to proximal tubular handling of filtered macromolecules, a process that is central to proteinuric kidney injury and tubular dysfunction. Impairment of this endocytic machinery can contribute to urinary loss of low-molecular-weight proteins, altered vitamin and iron metabolism, and tubular stress responses. The fact that CBLIF acts with LRP2, a major proximal tubular scavenger receptor system, further strengthens its relevance to chronic kidney disease mechanisms involving defective tubular reabsorption, protein overload, and epithelial injury. Thus, among the proteins listed, CBLIF stands out as a mechanistically compelling candidate for involvement in renal tubular disease and broader kidney pathophysiology.[PubMed:10371504](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10371504) [PubMed:11606717](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11606717) [PubMed:11717447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11717447) [PubMed:14576052](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14576052) [PubMed:9572993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9572993) 

In parallel with proximal tubular endocytic mechanisms, vascular and inflammatory pathways may also contribute importantly to renal injury. AOC3 is highly relevant to kidney disease because it links vascular inflammation with reactive metabolite generation. Its enzymatic activity produces hydrogen peroxide and aldehydes, both of which can promote oxidative stress and endothelial injury, processes that are well established in chronic kidney disease, diabetic nephropathy, and inflammatory renal disorders. In parallel, its endothelial adhesion function supports leukocyte recruitment and tissue infiltration, suggesting a role in renal inflammatory cell trafficking. These dual properties make AOC3 particularly interesting in diseases characterized by endothelial dysfunction, interstitial inflammation, and progressive fibrosis. In the kidney microvasculature, sustained AOC3 activity could plausibly amplify inflammatory signaling and oxidative damage, thereby contributing to both glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury.

Consistent with this vascular theme, proteins involved in endothelial organization and remodeling may also be relevant. JAM3 is notable because endothelial migration and angiogenesis are central to renal vascular homeostasis and disease progression. In kidney disease, especially diabetic kidney disease, ischemic nephropathy, and fibrotic remodeling, abnormalities in endothelial repair and microvascular integrity are major determinants of outcome. A protein that promotes endothelial chemotaxis and angiogenesis may influence capillary remodeling, glomerular endothelial responses, and the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive neovascularization. Although the annotation here is concise, the vascular emphasis of JAM3 makes it a plausible contributor to renal microvascular dysfunction, which is increasingly recognized as a driver of chronic kidney disease progression.

From vascular regulation, the discussion naturally extends to growth factor signaling pathways that may shape injury responses across multiple renal compartments. KITLG stands out because it controls multiple core signaling pathways that govern cell survival, proliferation, and tissue repair. These pathways, including phosphoinositide 3-kinase and protein kinase B, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling, are highly relevant to renal epithelial survival, interstitial cell activation, and inflammatory responses. In kidney disease, dysregulated growth factor signaling can shape tubular regeneration after injury, fibroblast activation, and immune cell behavior. KITLG is also important in hematopoiesis and mast cell biology, which may be relevant to renal inflammation and immune-mediated injury. While its role is likely context dependent, KITLG represents a biologically meaningful candidate for modulating kidney injury responses, particularly where repair, inflammation, and maladaptive remodeling intersect.

Alongside growth and repair signaling, immune cell trafficking and clearance mechanisms may provide an additional layer of relevance. CD302 is of interest in kidney disease because endocytosis, phagocytosis, and leukocyte or resident immune-cell migration are all relevant to renal inflammation and clearance of cellular debris. In injured kidneys, macrophages, dendritic cells, and other myeloid populations contribute to both tissue damage and repair. A receptor with potential roles in phagocytosis and adhesion may influence how immune cells traffic into renal tissue and respond to injury. Although the functional annotation is broad, its immunologic and endocytic properties suggest possible involvement in inflammatory kidney diseases and in the regulation of tubulointerstitial immune responses.

A related but somewhat more indirect connection may involve susceptibility to infection-associated renal injury. CXADR is relevant primarily through a potential link to infection-associated kidney injury. Viral receptor expression can shape tissue tropism and susceptibility to direct or indirect organ damage. Although the annotation provided focuses on microbial infection rather than intrinsic renal biology, viral infections can trigger glomerular or tubulointerstitial injury through direct cytopathic effects or immune-mediated mechanisms. Therefore, CXADR may be important in settings where viral exposure contributes to renal pathology, even if its kidney-specific role is less direct than that of tubular endocytic or vascular inflammatory proteins.

Returning to structural biology, several proteins in the enriched set may be relevant through their roles in membrane stability and cytoskeletal organization. DMD is potentially relevant to kidney disease because maintenance of membrane integrity and cytoskeletal linkage to the extracellular matrix are fundamental to epithelial and specialized filtration cell function. In the kidney, analogous structural systems are critical for podocyte architecture and tubular epithelial stability. Although DMD is best known for its role in muscle and synaptic tissues, its annotated function highlights mechanisms—membrane stabilization, cytoskeletal anchoring, and extracellular matrix interaction—that are highly pertinent to renal injury biology. Disruption of such structural networks can contribute to mechanosensitivity, cell detachment, and tissue remodeling, all of which are relevant in chronic kidney disease.

This emphasis on structural organization is further reinforced by proteins that regulate actin-dependent contractility. ACTA2 is relevant to kidney disease because actin dynamics are central to vascular smooth muscle function, mesangial contraction, and myofibroblast-mediated fibrosis. In renal disease, activation of contractile and migratory cell programs contributes to vascular remodeling and interstitial scarring. Although the annotation is general, the involvement of actin in cell motility and contractility makes ACTA2 particularly interesting in the context of fibrogenesis and altered renal hemodynamics. Increased smooth muscle-like or myofibroblast phenotypes are common features of progressive kidney injury, and proteins governing this cytoskeletal machinery are therefore biologically important.

In a similar manner, proteins that organize actin filament architecture may also influence renal cell resilience. ACTN2 may have indirect relevance to kidney disease through its role in organizing the actin cytoskeleton. Renal epithelial cells, podocytes, and vascular cells depend on highly ordered actin networks to maintain barrier function, adhesion, and mechanical resilience. Cytoskeletal disorganization is a hallmark of several kidney diseases, especially those involving podocyte injury and proteinuria. While ACTN2 is not specifically annotated here as a renal protein, its function in actin cross-linking suggests potential importance in maintaining cellular architecture under mechanical and inflammatory stress conditions encountered in diseased kidneys.

Extending this cytoskeletal perspective, proteins involved in membrane ruffling and dynamic remodeling may be particularly relevant during epithelial repair. EPS8L2 is potentially relevant because membrane ruffling and actin remodeling are integral to epithelial migration, repair, and barrier maintenance. In kidney injury, cytoskeletal remodeling influences tubular epithelial dedifferentiation, migration during regeneration, and in some contexts maladaptive changes in cell shape and adhesion. Through effects on SOS1-linked signaling and actin dynamics, EPS8L2 may participate in pathways that determine whether renal epithelial responses favor repair or progression toward fibrosis. Its connection is less direct than that of proximal tubular receptors or endothelial inflammatory mediators, but it remains mechanistically interesting.

Beyond cytoskeletal remodeling alone, membrane trafficking pathways may also intersect with metabolic stress in kidney disease. STX4 is noteworthy because insulin signaling and glucose transport are highly relevant to metabolic kidney disease, particularly diabetic nephropathy. Vesicle docking and membrane fusion machinery can influence how cells respond to insulin and regulate glucose handling. Although the annotation is centered on adipocytes, the broader implication is that STX4 participates in membrane trafficking pathways that may affect renal cellular metabolism and insulin responsiveness. Given the central role of insulin resistance and metabolic stress in chronic kidney disease, STX4 may represent an indirect but potentially meaningful link to kidney pathogenesis.

Finally, another membrane-associated regulator in the enriched set may have a more tentative but still potentially informative connection to renal cell morphology. PALM has a more speculative connection to kidney disease, but its role in plasma membrane dynamics and cell process formation may still be relevant. Renal epithelial cells and podocytes rely on specialized membrane protrusions and dynamic cortical structures to maintain filtration and absorptive functions. Proteins that regulate membrane architecture can therefore influence cellular resilience and morphology during injury. However, based on the provided annotation, PALM appears less directly connected to kidney disease mechanisms than proteins involved in proximal tubular endocytosis, endothelial inflammation, or growth factor signaling.

### late endosome (GO:0005770) 

The late endosome is a prelysosomal compartment within the endocytic system that arises during the maturation of early endosomes. This organelle is characterized by progressive acidification of its lumen, remodeling of its membrane and luminal protein composition, and a shift in intracellular localization toward the perinuclear region near the microtubule organizing center. In comparison with early endosomes, late endosomes are generally more spherical and function as a critical sorting and trafficking station for internalized membrane proteins, lipids, receptors, and extracellular cargo. They participate in the delivery of material either toward lysosomal degradation, back to other intracellular compartments, or, in some contexts, toward exocytic release. Because they integrate endocytosis, membrane recycling, cargo degradation, and signaling attenuation, late endosomes are essential for maintaining cellular proteostasis, membrane composition, and receptor homeostasis. In highly polarized and metabolically active renal cells, especially proximal tubular epithelial cells and podocytes, efficient late endosomal maturation and trafficking are expected to be particularly important because these cells continuously internalize proteins and membrane components and rely on tightly regulated degradative pathways to preserve filtration barrier integrity and tubular reabsorptive function.

Building on this cell biological framework, the potential relevance of the pathway to kidney disease can be considered cautiously on mechanistic grounds. No pathway-specific publications were provided in the input list, so the relationship between the late endosome pathway and kidney disease cannot be attributed here to the supplied disease-focused studies. Nevertheless, based on the pathway definition and the cited foundational cell biological literature, the late endosome is plausibly relevant to kidney disease because renal cells depend heavily on endocytic trafficking, cargo sorting, and lysosome-directed degradation. Disturbance of late endosomal acidification, maturation, perinuclear trafficking, or cargo transfer to lysosomes would be expected to impair protein handling, receptor turnover, and membrane homeostasis in glomerular and tubular compartments. In the kidney, such defects could promote intracellular accumulation of filtered proteins, defective degradation of damaged membrane proteins, altered growth factor and inflammatory signaling, cellular stress, and progressive injury of podocytes and tubular epithelial cells, all of which are central processes in chronic kidney injury and proteinuric disease. Thus, although direct kidney disease publications were not supplied, the known biology of the late endosome supports a mechanistic link between dysfunction of this organelle and renal pathology through impaired endocytic processing and defective prelysosomal trafficking. This interpretation is supported only by the general pathway-defining references describing the identity, maturation state, acidity, morphology, and intracellular positioning of late endosomes.[PubMed:11964142](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11964142) [PubMed:2557062](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2557062) 

With this mechanistic context in place, the enrichment results provide a quantitative indication that kidney disease-associated proteins may converge on this compartment. There were 24 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the late endosome as a prelysosomal compartment within the endocytic system, indicating a quantitatively substantial convergence of kidney disease-related molecular signals on intracellular cargo sorting, lumen acidification, membrane remodeling, and degradative trafficking functions. This enrichment pattern is biologically notable because the pathway captures multiple tightly coordinated processes that are especially relevant to renal cell physiology, including endocytic maturation, receptor turnover, membrane homeostasis, and lysosome-directed cargo handling, all of which are expected to be highly active in proximal tubular epithelial cells and podocytes that continuously process large amounts of filtered proteins and membrane components. We include below the protein-protein interaction network visualization for these 24 proteins together with the direct link to the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes and Proteins webpage for interactive inspection of their connectivity structure.

To further interpret this enrichment pattern, the most significant proteins identified in the function enrichment analysis are introduced below in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

EGFR is one of the most compelling proteins in this list for kidney disease because EGFR signaling is centrally involved in renal epithelial repair, fibrosis, and progression of chronic kidney injury. The functional description provided here is particularly relevant because it emphasizes not only canonical receptor signaling but also ubiquitin-dependent control of receptor fate and downstream pathway intensity. In the kidney, excessive or sustained EGFR activation has been linked to tubular epithelial proliferation, inflammatory signaling, fibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix accumulation, all of which are key mechanisms in chronic kidney disease and maladaptive repair after acute kidney injury. The fact that EGFR can regulate MAPK activity and promote degradation of signaling intermediates suggests that altered receptor trafficking or ubiquitination could modulate whether EGFR signaling is protective and regenerative or instead pro-fibrotic. Thus, EGFR stands out as a mechanistically plausible mediator of renal injury progression and a potential therapeutic node in fibrotic and proliferative kidney disorders.

In a related but distinct way, the next protein connects late endosomal biology with lipid handling, epithelial transport, and proteostatic control. PCSK9 is highly relevant to kidney disease because it intersects several processes that are pathogenic in renal disorders, including dyslipidemia, tubular handling of membrane proteins, and sodium balance. Its best-established function is the degradation of LDLR family receptors, which is important because lipid abnormalities are common in chronic kidney disease and contribute to vascular injury, glomerular damage, and progressive renal dysfunction. Particularly noteworthy in the present annotation is its ability to reduce ENaC surface expression, since ENaC is a critical determinant of distal nephron sodium reabsorption, extracellular volume status, and hypertension, all of which strongly influence kidney disease progression. Its involvement in lysosomal and proteasomal routing further suggests broader effects on renal epithelial proteostasis. Therefore, PCSK9 stands out as a protein connecting metabolic, hemodynamic, and intracellular trafficking mechanisms that are all highly pertinent to kidney pathophysiology.[PubMed:18039658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18039658) [PubMed:17461796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17461796) [PubMed:18197702](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18197702) [PubMed:18799458](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18799458) [PubMed:22074827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22074827) [PubMed:18660751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18660751) 

Extending this theme of intracellular homeostasis, the following transporter suggests a possible link between metal handling, stress responses, and renal injury. SLC39A14 is especially interesting in the context of kidney disease because it links metal-ion transport to inflammation, metabolic regulation, and cellular stress responses. Renal tissue is highly sensitive to disturbances in zinc, iron, and manganese homeostasis, and the ability of SLC39A14 to transport cadmium is particularly relevant because cadmium is a well-known nephrotoxin associated with tubular injury and chronic renal damage. The annotation also indicates a role in endoplasmic reticulum stress adaptation and macrophage cytokine regulation, both of which are major drivers of kidney injury and fibrosis. In addition, its effects on insulin signaling and glucose metabolism may be relevant to diabetic kidney disease, where altered metal handling, oxidative stress, and metabolic dysfunction converge. Altogether, SLC39A14 stands out as a plausible contributor to kidney disease through toxic metal uptake, inflammatory regulation, and stress-response pathways.[PubMed:15642354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15642354) [PubMed:27231142](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27231142) [PubMed:29621230](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29621230) [PubMed:27703010](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27703010) [PubMed:31028174](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31028174) [PubMed:31699897](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31699897) [PubMed:20682781](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20682781) [PubMed:23052185](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23052185) 

Consistent with the importance of intracellular clearance pathways, the next protein further emphasizes the possible contribution of lysosomal stress responses to renal pathology. LAMP3 is relevant to kidney disease because lysosomal integrity, autophagic flux, and unfolded protein response signaling are fundamental determinants of renal tubular cell survival under stress. Kidney epithelial cells are continuously exposed to metabolic, toxic, and ischemic insults, and defects in autophagosome-lysosome fusion can exacerbate protein aggregation, organelle damage, and cell death. The annotation that LAMP3 contributes to survival during proteasomal dysfunction is particularly important, as proteostasis failure is increasingly recognized in acute kidney injury, diabetic nephropathy, and chronic kidney disease. By influencing both unfolded protein response and autophagy, LAMP3 may affect whether stressed renal cells recover or transition toward maladaptive injury and fibrosis. Its role therefore aligns closely with established mechanisms of renal degeneration driven by impaired intracellular clearance pathways.

Shifting from proteostatic stress to immune activation, the following protein suggests a possible interface between interferon signaling, epithelial organization, and tissue remodeling. BST2 is noteworthy for kidney disease primarily because of its strong connection to interferon signaling, antiviral defense, and nuclear factor kappa B activation. Viral infections and interferon-driven inflammation are established contributors to several renal pathologies, including virus-associated glomerulopathies and inflammatory tubulointerstitial injury. The ability of BST2 to shape type one interferon feedback and activate nuclear factor kappa B suggests that it may influence the intensity and duration of renal inflammatory responses. In addition, its effects on MMP14 and MMP15-related growth and migration could be relevant to tissue remodeling and fibrosis, while its role in epithelial actin organization may affect barrier properties in polarized renal epithelia. Thus, BST2 stands out as an immune-regulatory and epithelial structural factor with plausible relevance to inflammatory and infection-associated kidney injury.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:19179289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19179289) [PubMed:20686043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20686043) [PubMed:20943977](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20943977) [PubMed:21621240](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21621240) [PubMed:26378163](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26378163) [PubMed:31199522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31199522) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328) 

This immune-inflammatory perspective is complemented by a protein that more directly links coagulation signaling with renal inflammation and vascular injury. F2R is highly relevant to kidney disease because coagulation, endothelial activation, and inflammation are tightly interwoven in many renal syndromes. Thrombin signaling through F2R can promote calcium-dependent cellular activation and inflammatory cytokine production, and the induction of mediators such as CCL2 and IL6 is particularly pertinent because these cytokines are major drivers of leukocyte recruitment, renal inflammation, and fibrogenesis. In kidney disease, activation of coagulation pathways is observed in glomerular injury, diabetic nephropathy, thrombotic microangiopathy, and chronic fibrotic remodeling. F2R may therefore serve as a mechanistic bridge between hemostatic disturbances and inflammatory tissue damage within the kidney, especially in vascular and glomerular compartments.[PubMed:25645137](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25645137) 

Returning to endolysosomal trafficking itself, the next protein may be relevant because renal tubular homeostasis depends heavily on efficient delivery of degradative enzymes. IGF2R is potentially important in kidney disease because lysosomal enzyme trafficking is essential for renal tubular homeostasis, where high endocytic and degradative activity is required to process filtered proteins and maintain cellular integrity. Disruption of lysosomal targeting pathways can contribute to tubular dysfunction, protein handling defects, and progressive injury. Its capacity to bind IGF2 also suggests possible relevance to growth-factor regulation, which is important in renal hypertrophy and fibrotic remodeling. Furthermore, the link to T-cell coactivation raises the possibility that IGF2R may influence immune-mediated kidney injury. Although its renal role is less direct than that of EGFR or PCSK9, IGF2R stands out because defects in endolysosomal trafficking are increasingly recognized as important contributors to renal disease mechanisms.

Another protein in this set appears to converge on a similarly important axis of autophagy, redox control, and innate immune signaling. Based on the functions provided, this protein is highly relevant to kidney disease because it integrates autophagy, oxidative stress control, and innate immune signaling, which are all central to renal injury and progression. Selective autophagy is protective in podocytes and tubular epithelial cells, where it limits accumulation of damaged proteins and organelles. The described ability to modulate type one interferon responses and oxidative stress through the KEAP1-NRF2 axis is particularly important, since both inflammatory signaling and redox imbalance are major determinants of acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, and immune-mediated nephropathies. In addition, regulation of IL-12 trafficking and secretion suggests a role in shaping inflammatory immune responses that could affect renal tissue damage. Thus, the functional profile given here strongly supports relevance to kidney pathology through proteostasis and immunometabolic stress pathways.[PubMed:31916398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31916398) [PubMed:34374750](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34374750) 

In contrast to these broader stress-response functions, the following protein may act more specifically as a modifier of signaling intensity. RNF149 is of potential interest in kidney disease because BRAF is a key component of the MAPK signaling cascade, which regulates cell proliferation, survival, dedifferentiation, and fibrosis in renal cells. By promoting BRAF degradation, RNF149 may influence the amplitude or duration of MAPK pathway activation during kidney injury. This is relevant because excessive MAPK signaling has been implicated in tubular damage, cystic growth, and fibrotic remodeling. Although the annotation is concise, the function positions RNF149 as a possible regulator of renal stress signaling and epithelial plasticity, making it a plausible modifier of disease severity rather than a primary driver.

A similarly indirect but still potentially meaningful connection is suggested by the next lysosome-associated membrane protein. SCARB2 has a more indirect but still meaningful potential connection to kidney disease through infection biology and lysosomal membrane function. As a viral receptor, it may influence susceptibility to systemic viral infections that can secondarily affect the kidney through direct viral tropism, immune activation, or cytokine-mediated injury. In addition, SCARB2 is a lysosome-associated membrane protein family member, and lysosomal dysfunction is highly relevant to renal epithelial health. While the annotation here specifically emphasizes viral entry, this still makes SCARB2 noteworthy in the setting of infection-associated renal complications.

Finally, this infection- and interferon-related theme extends to a myeloid-associated immune mediator that may be relevant in inflammatory nephropathies. SIGLEC1 is relevant to kidney disease mainly through immune and infection-associated mechanisms. Dendritic cell activation and viral handling can shape systemic and tissue-specific inflammatory responses, including those affecting the kidney. In disorders where viral infection precipitates glomerular or tubulointerstitial injury, proteins that enhance viral capture or transfer may influence disease initiation or severity. Because SIGLEC1 is also a marker of interferon-activated myeloid cells, its function is consistent with pathways that are often upregulated in lupus nephritis and other interferon-driven renal diseases. Therefore, although not kidney-specific, SIGLEC1 stands out as an immune mediator with plausible relevance to inflammatory nephropathies.

### carboxylic acid binding (GO:0031406) 

Carboxylic acid binding is a molecular function that refers to the selective and non covalent interaction of a protein with carboxylic acids, a broad chemical class that includes many endogenous metabolites and signaling molecules containing one or more carboxyl groups. In biology, this functional category encompasses proteins that recognize free fatty acids, amino acids, tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, bile acid related molecules, uric acid related compounds, and numerous organic anions that circulate in blood or are generated during intermediary metabolism. Carboxylic acid binding is therefore not a single linear signaling pathway, but rather a biochemical interaction module that contributes to metabolite sensing, ligand transport, enzymatic catalysis, transcriptional regulation, and detoxification. In the kidney, this function is particularly important because renal tissue is continuously exposed to filtered and secreted organic acids and must coordinate their uptake, intracellular handling, metabolism, and excretion. Proteins with carboxylic acid binding activity can influence tubular transport processes, mitochondrial energy metabolism, lipid handling, oxidative stress responses, and inflammatory signaling. Because the kidney is a major organ for maintaining systemic acid base balance and for clearing many endogenous and exogenous organic acids, perturbation of proteins that bind carboxylic acids may alter metabolic homeostasis, promote tubular injury, and contribute to chronic or acute forms of kidney disease.

Against this biological background, the current evidence set should be interpreted cautiously. No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a literature supported pathway to kidney disease cannot be directly inferred from the supplied evidence set. Nevertheless, from a biological perspective, carboxylic acid binding is plausibly related to kidney disease because the kidney is a central organ for the filtration, reabsorption, secretion, and metabolic processing of carboxyl containing compounds, including fatty acids and other organic acids. Disturbance of proteins that bind such ligands could influence proximal tubular handling of filtered metabolites, mitochondrial substrate utilization, lipid accumulation, oxidative injury, inflammatory activation, and the retention of protein bound organic acids during impaired renal function. These processes are broadly relevant to diabetic kidney disease, ischemic tubular injury, toxin associated nephropathy, and chronic kidney disease progression. However, because no publications were supplied, any specific mechanistic claim, disease association, or causal interpretation would be insufficiently supported in the present analysis and should be regarded as a hypothesis requiring confirmation from primary literature.

With that limitation in mind, the enrichment results still provide a useful framework for interpretation. There were 30 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the molecular function of carboxylic acid binding. This functional category captures the selective and non covalent interaction between proteins and carboxylic acids, a chemically broad group that includes free fatty acids, amino acids, tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, bile acid related molecules, uric acid related compounds, and many additional organic anions generated during metabolism or transported in blood. In the context of kidney disease, enrichment of 30 proteins in this function is biologically notable because the kidney is one of the principal organs responsible for filtering, secreting, reabsorbing, metabolizing, and excreting endogenous and exogenous organic acids. A set of this size supports the interpretation that metabolite recognition and handling are not peripheral events, but rather a central biochemical theme in renal pathophysiology.

This enrichment also appears to align with several interrelated aspects of renal injury biology. The functional implications of carboxylic acid binding in kidney disease extend across several tightly connected processes. Proteins in this category can regulate tubular transport of organic acids, intracellular metabolite trafficking, mitochondrial energy metabolism, lipid handling, oxidative stress responses, inflammatory signaling, and detoxification capacity. Because renal tissue is continuously exposed to large quantities of filtered solutes, even modest perturbation in proteins that bind carboxylic acids can alter acid base homeostasis, disrupt intermediary metabolism, and increase susceptibility to tubular injury. The presence of 30 enriched proteins therefore suggests a broad systems level disturbance rather than an isolated molecular event, linking metabolic sensing and organic acid handling to both chronic and acute forms of kidney disease.

To further contextualize these observations, the interaction structure of the enriched proteins is shown below. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 30 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is also provided for interactive inspection. Many of these involved proteins have known functions related to renal metabolism, solute transport, and injury responses in kidney disease. We will introduce them in details in the following.
