Building on this network-level view, the following paragraphs summarize several significant proteins identified during the enrichment analysis. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

FOLR1 is one of the most directly kidney-relevant proteins in this list because its annotated function explicitly includes a requirement for renal folate reabsorption. This places FOLR1 at the intersection of tubular epithelial transport, nutrient conservation, and epithelial cell homeostasis. In the context of kidney disease, impaired folate handling can contribute to metabolic stress, defective cellular proliferation and repair, and altered one-carbon metabolism, all of which may influence susceptibility to tubular injury and recovery capacity. Its role in receptor-mediated endocytosis and pH-dependent folate release is also mechanistically relevant to proximal tubular function, where receptor-mediated reclamation of filtered solutes is a core physiological process. Therefore, FOLR1 stands out as a protein with a direct physiological connection to renal function and a plausible contribution to kidney disease when folate transport or epithelial integrity is disrupted.[PubMed:1894617](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1894617) [PubMed:10508523](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10508523) [PubMed:12854656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12854656) [PubMed:15259034](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15259034) [PubMed:17286298](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17286298) [PubMed:15703271](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15703271) 

A transition from tubular nutrient handling to glomerular integrity highlights the breadth of kidney-relevant processes represented in this enriched set. PLA2G1B is highly relevant to kidney disease because its function is explicitly linked to podocyte survival and glomerular homeostasis through interaction with PLA2R1. Podocytes are essential components of the glomerular filtration barrier, and their injury or loss is a central event in proteinuric kidney diseases, including membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. The annotation suggests that PLA2G1B is not merely a digestive phospholipase but also a signaling molecule capable of influencing renal cell survival pathways. Its autocrine/paracrine activity and effects on lipid mediators further support a role in inflammatory and metabolic signaling within the kidney. Given that glomerular dysfunction is a major determinant of chronic kidney disease progression, PLA2G1B represents one of the strongest candidates in this list for mechanistic relevance to renal pathology.[PubMed:10681567](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10681567) [PubMed:1420353](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1420353) [PubMed:17603006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17603006) [PubMed:25335547](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25335547) [PubMed:7721806](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7721806) 

From glomerular homeostasis, the analysis then shifts toward injury response and tissue remodeling. MDK (midkine) is among the most compelling kidney disease-associated proteins in this dataset because its annotation directly mentions epithelial cell survival after renal damage and broad roles in inflammation, regeneration, and cell migration. These processes are central to both acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease progression. MDK can recruit neutrophils and macrophages to sites of tissue injury, induce chemokine expression, and activate MAPK and AKT survival pathways, indicating that it may shape both the inflammatory and reparative phases of renal injury. While such actions may support tissue regeneration, persistent or dysregulated MDK signaling could also promote maladaptive repair, fibrosis-associated inflammation, or epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition through NOTCH2-related mechanisms. Its involvement in angiogenesis and vascular responses is additionally relevant because microvascular rarefaction and endothelial dysfunction are major contributors to progressive renal injury. Collectively, MDK stands out as a multifunctional mediator with strong plausibility in kidney injury, repair, and chronic disease remodeling.[PubMed:10212223](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10212223) [PubMed:10772929](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10772929) [PubMed:12084985](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12084985) [PubMed:12122009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12122009) [PubMed:12573468](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12573468) [PubMed:15466886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15466886) [PubMed:18469519](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18469519) [PubMed:24458438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24458438) [PubMed:10683378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10683378) [PubMed:22323540](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22323540) 

A related theme emerging from the dataset is the contribution of innate immunity to renal injury. FCN1 is relevant to kidney disease because complement activation and innate immune sensing are major drivers of inflammatory renal injury. As a lectin pathway activator, FCN1 may contribute to complement-mediated tissue damage in settings such as infection-associated kidney injury, immune-mediated glomerulonephritis, and systemic inflammatory states that secondarily affect the kidney. Its ability to activate monocytes and induce IL-8 secretion further links it to leukocyte recruitment and amplification of intrarenal inflammation. These functions are particularly important because the kidney is highly vulnerable to injury from excessive complement activation and inflammatory cell infiltration. Thus, FCN1 stands out as a plausible mediator of renal inflammation, especially in diseases where innate immunity and complement dysregulation are pathogenic.

Continuing within the immune regulatory dimension, CD33 is potentially relevant to kidney disease through its role as an inhibitory immune receptor that restrains monocyte activation. Monocytes and macrophages are central participants in acute kidney injury, chronic interstitial inflammation, and fibrotic progression. By recruiting SHP-1 and SHP-2 phosphatases after ligand engagement, CD33 dampens signaling cascades that would otherwise promote inflammatory activation. This suggests that CD33 may influence the threshold for innate immune activation in renal inflammatory disorders. In disease settings characterized by sterile inflammation, immune complex deposition, or chronic tissue injury, altered CD33 signaling could modulate the balance between protective immune quiescence and damaging myeloid-cell activation. For this reason, CD33 is noteworthy as a regulator of inflammatory tone with plausible importance in kidney disease pathogenesis.[PubMed:10611343](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10611343) [PubMed:11320212](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11320212) [PubMed:15597323](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15597323) [PubMed:7718872](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7718872) [PubMed:10887109](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10887109) [PubMed:28325905](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28325905) [PubMed:10206955](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10206955) [PubMed:10556798](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10556798) 

In parallel with immune signaling, lipid mediator biology may also be relevant to the observed enrichment pattern. PTGDS is relevant to kidney disease because prostaglandin signaling is a major determinant of renal hemodynamics, vascular tone, inflammatory signaling, and tubular function. By generating PGD2, PTGDS may influence intrarenal blood flow, platelet activity, and inflammatory cell behavior, all of which are important in acute and chronic renal injury. Its additional capacity to bind and transport hydrophobic molecules suggests a protective role in handling potentially toxic lipophilic compounds. Since the kidney is particularly sensitive to changes in microvascular tone and inflammatory lipid mediators, PTGDS may contribute to both adaptive and maladaptive responses during renal stress. Although the annotation emphasizes central nervous system and barrier functions, the enzymatic generation of prostaglandins provides a biologically credible connection to kidney pathophysiology.[PubMed:20667974](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20667974) [PubMed:9475419](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9475419) 

This connection to lipid-associated processes is further reinforced by proteins involved in systemic lipoprotein handling. APOC1 is of interest in kidney disease primarily because lipid dysregulation is a major contributor to chronic kidney disease progression and cardiovascular complications in renal patients. By modulating lipoprotein receptor interactions, fatty acid uptake, and cholesteryl ester transfer, APOC1 may influence systemic and possibly renal lipid handling. Lipid accumulation in renal cells, particularly in glomerular and tubular compartments, has been implicated in lipotoxicity, inflammation, and fibrosis. Therefore, APOC1 may be mechanistically relevant in metabolic kidney disease, including diabetic kidney disease and obesity-associated nephropathy, where altered lipoprotein metabolism exacerbates renal injury. Although the annotation does not directly mention the kidney, its central role in lipid transport and fatty acid biology makes it a plausible modifier of renal disease susceptibility and progression.

Alongside metabolic and inflammatory mechanisms, protease regulation and vascular integrity also appear relevant. AMBP is potentially relevant to kidney disease because coagulation, protease activity, and inflammatory mast cell proteases all contribute to renal injury and microvascular dysfunction. The kidney is highly dependent on intact microcirculation, and dysregulated coagulation can promote glomerular and peritubular capillary injury, especially in thrombotic microangiopathy, sepsis-associated kidney injury, and inflammatory nephropathies. By inhibiting factor Xa and other serine proteases, AMBP may influence the balance between thrombosis, inflammation, and tissue injury. In addition, inhibition of chymase and tryptase suggests possible effects on mast cell-driven inflammatory remodeling, which has been implicated in renal fibrosis. Thus, AMBP stands out as a protease-regulatory molecule with plausible importance in renal vascular and inflammatory pathology.

The immune-regulatory component of the enriched set extends further to additional sialic acid-binding receptors. SIGLEC7 may be relevant to kidney disease because it functions as an inhibitory immune receptor capable of suppressing cytotoxic and myeloid-cell responses. In renal disease, especially transplant injury, autoimmune nephritis, and inflammatory kidney disorders, the magnitude of innate immune activation can strongly influence tissue damage. By attenuating NK-cell cytotoxicity and modulating hematopoietic differentiation, SIGLEC7 may affect the composition and activation state of immune infiltrates within the kidney. Since sialylation patterns often change during tissue injury and inflammation, SIGLEC7-mediated recognition of altered glycans could contribute to immunoregulation in diseased renal tissue. Its importance is therefore likely indirect but mechanistically meaningful in immune-mediated kidney pathology.

Finally, a related glycan-sensitive immune mechanism is represented by SIGLEC8. SIGLEC8 is a potentially interesting kidney-related candidate because glycan-dependent immune cell trafficking and activation are increasingly recognized as contributors to renal inflammation. Its selective recognition of sulfated sialylated glycans suggests a role in fine-tuning leukocyte interactions in inflamed tissues. Although the annotation does not directly connect SIGLEC8 to renal biology, kidney disease often involves altered endothelial glycocalyx composition, leukocyte recruitment, and eosinophil- or other leukocyte-associated inflammatory responses. In that context, SIGLEC8 may be relevant as a marker or regulator of glycan-mediated immune processes that influence renal injury.[PubMed:10625619](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10625619) [PubMed:10856141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10856141) [PubMed:27357658](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27357658)

### calcium ion binding (GO:0005509) 

Calcium ion binding is a molecular function that describes the selective and non-covalent interaction of a protein or other biomolecule with calcium ions. This property is fundamental to cellular physiology because calcium ions act as versatile second messengers and structural cofactors in many biological processes. Proteins with calcium ion binding capacity include extracellular matrix proteins, membrane-associated proteins, signaling adaptors, cytoskeletal regulators, channels, transport-related proteins, and enzymes whose conformation and activity are altered by calcium occupancy. In the kidney, calcium ion binding is especially important because renal epithelial cells continuously regulate mineral balance, transcellular transport, tubular reabsorption, cell polarity, mechanosensation, and responses to injury. Calcium ion binding proteins participate in filtration barrier integrity, tubular transport, mitochondrial function, oxidative stress responses, inflammatory signaling, apoptosis, and tissue remodeling. Disturbance of calcium handling or of proteins that bind calcium ions can therefore influence nephron development, glomerular and tubular homeostasis, crystal formation, fibrotic remodeling, and progression of both acute and chronic forms of kidney disease.

Building on this biological context, the relevance of this molecular function to kidney disease can be considered even in the absence of a directly supplied literature set for pathway-level synthesis. No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a literature-supported pathway-to-disease synthesis cannot be derived from the supplied evidence set. Nevertheless, from established biological principles, calcium ion binding is highly relevant to kidney disease because the kidney is a central organ for calcium homeostasis and because many renal cell processes depend on calcium-sensitive proteins. In glomerular cells and tubular epithelial cells, calcium ion binding proteins help regulate membrane excitability, cytoskeletal organization, vesicular trafficking, mitochondrial metabolism, and transcriptional responses to stress. When calcium signaling becomes dysregulated during ischemic injury, toxic injury, metabolic stress, crystal exposure, or chronic inflammatory states, abnormal activation or failure of calcium ion binding proteins can promote epithelial damage, cell death, barrier dysfunction, and profibrotic signaling. In addition, extracellular calcium-binding matrix proteins may influence calcification, crystal retention, and interstitial remodeling, all of which are relevant to nephrolithiasis and chronic kidney disease progression. Because no publications were supplied, these statements should be interpreted as a mechanistic overview rather than a publication-based conclusion specific to the provided evidence.

This general framework is also consistent with the quantitative enrichment result obtained in the present analysis. There were 56 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the molecular function of calcium ion binding, a process that describes the selective and non-covalent interaction between biomolecules and calcium ions and that is highly relevant to renal physiology and pathology. This enrichment highlights a substantial protein set linked to calcium-dependent regulation in the kidney, where calcium-responsive molecules contribute to mineral balance, tubular reabsorption, epithelial polarity, mechanosensation, mitochondrial homeostasis, oxidative stress responses, inflammatory signaling, apoptosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and progression of both acute and chronic kidney disease. Given that the enriched set contains 56 proteins, the analysis supports a broad and quantitatively substantial involvement of calcium ion binding functions in kidney disease biology, consistent with the central role of calcium-mediated signaling and structural regulation across glomerular and tubular compartments.

To complement this enrichment result, the interaction structure of the identified protein set is shown below. The figure below presents the protein-protein interaction network of these 56 proteins, together with the link to the STRING webpage for interactive exploration.

During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

To move from the global enrichment pattern to individual components that may be especially informative, the following paragraphs summarize proteins whose annotations appear particularly relevant to kidney disease biology.

PKD2 is the most directly kidney-relevant protein in this list because its annotated function explicitly links it to primary cilium-dependent mechanosensation in renal epithelium, a central process in cystic kidney disease biology. Defects in PKD2-mediated ciliary signaling are a well-established mechanism underlying autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, in which altered sensing of tubular flow and dysregulated calcium homeostasis promote epithelial proliferation, cyst expansion, and progressive renal dysfunction. The functional annotation further indicates that PKD2 influences ER calcium handling and interacts with multiple calcium-permeable channels, suggesting that its pathogenic impact likely extends beyond ciliary signaling to broader control of epithelial signaling, tubular architecture, and vascular tone. Its additional role in regulating systemic blood pressure is also highly relevant, because hypertension is both a common manifestation and a disease modifier in chronic kidney disease.[PubMed:11854751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11854751) [PubMed:11991947](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11991947) [PubMed:15692563](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15692563) [PubMed:26269590](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26269590) [PubMed:27071085](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27071085) [PubMed:31441214](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31441214) [PubMed:39009345](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39009345) [PubMed:33164752](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33164752) [PubMed:27214281](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27214281) [PubMed:29899465](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29899465) [PubMed:18695040](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18695040) 

From this epithelial and calcium-signaling perspective, it is useful to next consider proteins that may be more closely related to vascular protection and endothelial homeostasis in the kidney.

THBD is highly relevant to kidney disease because glomerular and microvascular injury are strongly shaped by the balance between coagulation and endothelial inflammation. In the kidney, endothelial dysfunction contributes to thrombotic microangiopathy, sepsis-associated acute kidney injury, diabetic nephropathy, and progressive chronic kidney disease. The annotation indicates that THBD not only supports the activated protein C anticoagulant pathway but also reduces endothelial permeability and inflammatory signaling, including HMGB1-mediated responses. These functions are particularly important in the renal microcirculation, where excessive thrombin signaling, capillary leak, and inflammatory endothelial activation can precipitate ischemia, proteinuria, and fibrosis. Thus, THBD stands out as a mechanistically important protector of vascular homeostasis in kidney injury states.[PubMed:38174561](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38174561) 

A related but distinct aspect of kidney disease biology involves glomerular barrier maintenance and podocyte survival.

PLA2G1B is notable because its annotation explicitly connects it to podocyte survival and glomerular homeostasis through PLA2R1 signaling, directly implicating it in kidney biology. Podocytes are essential components of the glomerular filtration barrier, and their injury or loss is a major driver of proteinuria and progressive glomerulosclerosis. A protein that modulates podocyte survival is therefore immediately relevant to kidney disease pathogenesis. In addition, phospholipase-mediated lipid remodeling can influence inflammatory signaling and membrane integrity, processes that are increasingly recognized in glomerular injury. Given the centrality of podocyte dysfunction to many nephropathies, PLA2G1B merits attention as a potential regulator of glomerular resilience or injury.[PubMed:10681567](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10681567) [PubMed:1420353](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1420353) [PubMed:17603006](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17603006) [PubMed:25335547](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25335547) [PubMed:7721806](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7721806) 

Alongside glomerular injury, inflammatory endothelial activation and leukocyte recruitment are also recurring themes in many forms of renal disease.

AOC3 is relevant to kidney disease because it links endothelial inflammation with leukocyte recruitment, both of which are central to many renal disorders including glomerulonephritis, diabetic kidney disease, and allograft inflammation. Its enzymatic activity generates hydrogen peroxide and reactive aldehydes, which can amplify oxidative stress and endothelial injury, while its adhesion function promotes immune cell trafficking into tissues. In the kidney, such mechanisms may contribute to tubulointerstitial inflammation and vascular dysfunction, thereby accelerating chronic injury and fibrosis. The dual catalytic and adhesive properties of AOC3 make it particularly interesting as a mediator of inflammatory renal microenvironment remodeling.

This inflammatory recruitment theme may extend further to additional proteins involved in leukocyte movement across tissue barriers.

Although the annotation for ADAM8 is brief, its potential role in leukocyte extravasation makes it relevant to kidney disease, particularly inflammatory and immune-mediated nephropathies. Recruitment of circulating leukocytes into glomerular and interstitial compartments is a major pathogenic event in acute kidney injury, crescentic glomerulonephritis, lupus nephritis, and chronic interstitial fibrosis. A protein that facilitates leukocyte transmigration may therefore contribute to the initiation or amplification of renal inflammation. ADAM8 is especially notable because protease-adhesion molecules often participate in both immune-cell trafficking and matrix remodeling, two closely linked processes in progressive kidney injury.

Innate immune sensing provides another layer through which calcium ion binding proteins may intersect with renal injury pathways.

CLEC6A stands out because it integrates innate immune sensing, myeloid activation, and downstream inflammatory signaling pathways that are highly relevant to kidney injury. Activation of SYK, CARD9, and NF-kappa-B is mechanistically important in sterile and infectious renal inflammation, including tubulointerstitial nephritis and sepsis-associated acute kidney injury. Its association with neutrophil and platelet activation is also notable, as these cell types contribute to microvascular injury, immunothrombosis, and endothelial dysfunction in the kidney. Therefore, CLEC6A may be functionally connected to renal disease through amplification of innate immune responses and inflammatory vascular injury.[PubMed:14764707](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14764707) [PubMed:19098920](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19098920) [PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:17086186](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17086186) [PubMed:9171347](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9171347) 

Inflammation in the kidney is also closely coupled to lipid mediator signaling and fibrotic remodeling, which makes the next protein especially noteworthy.

ENPP2 is of substantial interest in kidney disease because the autotaxin-LPA axis is widely implicated in inflammation, fibrosis, vascular remodeling, and cell migration. The annotation emphasizes its ability to generate LPA, a potent bioactive lipid that can stimulate proliferation, motility, and angiogenic responses. In the kidney, these processes are highly relevant to tubulointerstitial fibrosis, mesangial activation, endothelial remodeling, and maladaptive repair after acute injury. Its role in platelet-derived LPA production may further connect it to microvascular dysfunction and inflammatory signaling within the renal circulation. Thus, ENPP2 is a plausible mediator of both chronic fibrotic progression and acute inflammatory remodeling in kidney disease.[PubMed:12354767](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12354767) [PubMed:14500380](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14500380) [PubMed:15769751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15769751) [PubMed:26371182](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26371182) [PubMed:27754931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27754931) [PubMed:12176993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12176993) [PubMed:11559573](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11559573) [PubMed:1733949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1733949) [PubMed:21393252](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21393252) 

Given the importance of fibrosis and maladaptive repair, extracellular matrix turnover becomes a logical next focus.

MMP13 is relevant to kidney disease because extracellular matrix turnover and growth factor activation are central determinants of renal fibrosis and maladaptive repair. The annotation indicates that MMP13 can degrade multiple matrix substrates and modulate key profibrotic regulators such as TGFB1 and CCN2, both of which are strongly implicated in chronic kidney disease progression. In the injured kidney, dysregulated matrix proteolysis can either facilitate repair or promote structural damage, basement membrane disruption, and fibrotic remodeling depending on context. MMP13 therefore stands out as a candidate effector of renal extracellular matrix reorganization during both acute and chronic disease.

A closely related matrix-remodeling protease in this enriched set is MMP12.

MMP12 is potentially important in kidney disease because tissue remodeling and matrix degradation are core features of inflammatory renal injury and fibrosis. Its elastolytic activity suggests a capacity to alter vascular and interstitial extracellular matrix architecture, which could influence renal perfusion, inflammatory cell infiltration, and fibrotic progression. Although the annotation is concise, MMP12 is especially relevant in settings where macrophage-driven proteolysis contributes to chronic injury. In the kidney, such remodeling can exacerbate capillary rarefaction and interstitial scarring, thereby promoting functional decline.

Beyond matrix degradation, matrix organization and cell survival may also be influenced by calcium-binding extracellular proteins.

COMP is relevant to kidney disease because matrix integrity, cell survival, and vascular smooth muscle phenotype are all important in renal fibrosis and vascular complications of chronic kidney disease. Its interactions with collagens and fibronectin suggest a role in matrix organization, while its anti-apoptotic activity may influence survival of resident stromal or vascular cells under stress. The ability of COMP to preserve a contractile vascular smooth muscle phenotype is particularly notable given the importance of vascular remodeling and arterial stiffness in CKD. Accordingly, COMP may contribute to both structural matrix remodeling and the vascular pathology that accompanies renal disease progression.[PubMed:16051604](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16051604) [PubMed:16542502](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16542502) [PubMed:17993464](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17993464) 

Cell-matrix adhesion pathways may provide an additional bridge between extracellular remodeling and renal structural adaptation.

Although the provided annotation for ITGA5 is limited, integrin alpha-5 is still potentially relevant to kidney disease because integrin-mediated cell-matrix interactions are fundamental to podocyte adhesion, mesangial behavior, endothelial signaling, and fibrotic remodeling. The explicit mention of angiogenesis is also noteworthy, as abnormal angiogenic and matrix-adhesive signaling can contribute to glomerular and interstitial remodeling. While this entry does not provide kidney-specific detail, ITGA5 remains of interest because integrin signaling broadly regulates adhesion-dependent survival and matrix responses in renal cells.

Inflammatory lipid metabolism is also represented by another phospholipase that may be relevant to acute injury and tissue repair.

PLA2G2A is highly relevant to kidney disease because it links innate immune activation, lipid mediator generation, platelet-associated inflammation, and tissue regeneration. The annotation highlights its ability to process extracellular mitochondrial membranes released during sterile inflammation, thereby generating arachidonate for leukotriene synthesis and promoting release of danger-associated molecules. These mechanisms are potentially important in acute kidney injury, where platelet activation, mitochondrial damage, and innate immune amplification are prominent. Its integrin-activating function may further influence cell proliferation and repair responses. Overall, PLA2G2A appears well positioned to modulate inflammatory and regenerative pathways that shape renal injury outcomes.[PubMed:10358193](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10358193) [PubMed:11694541](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11694541) [PubMed:8425615](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8425615) [PubMed:27292189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27292189) 

Several members of the S100 protein family in this enriched set further reinforce the connection between calcium binding and inflammatory tissue injury.

S100A12 is strongly connected to kidney disease through its role as a damage-associated inflammatory mediator. Activation of RAGE, MAPK, and NF-kappa-B signaling is highly relevant to diabetic kidney disease, chronic inflammation, and vascular injury, while induction of ICAM1 and VCAM1 can enhance leukocyte recruitment into renal tissue. In addition, its chemoattractant activity and capacity to amplify innate immune responses make it a plausible driver of tubulointerstitial inflammation. Because chronic kidney disease is often characterized by persistent sterile inflammation and endothelial activation, S100A12 stands out as a potentially important mediator linking tissue damage to progressive renal dysfunction.

A related but somewhat more dual-function inflammatory and reparative profile is suggested for S100A11.

S100A11 is relevant to kidney disease because leukocyte trafficking, inflammatory resolution, and tissue repair are key determinants of renal outcome after injury. Its ability to attract granulocytes and monocytes suggests a role in early inflammatory recruitment, whereas its association with wound healing implies a possible function in repair and recovery. In the kidney, these dual actions could be important in acute kidney injury, where the balance between inflammatory damage and reparative resolution influences progression to chronic fibrosis. Thus, S100A11 may represent a regulator of both injurious and restorative immune responses in renal tissue.[PubMed:15187149](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15187149) [PubMed:22879591](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22879591) [PubMed:25664854](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25664854) 

This balance between inflammation and fibrosis is also relevant to S100A4.

S100A4 is notable in kidney disease because it combines profibrotic cellular features—enhanced motility, altered apoptosis, and inflammatory cytokine induction—with immune cell chemotactic activity. These properties are relevant to fibroblast activation, epithelial plasticity, inflammatory infiltration, and interstitial remodeling, all of which are central to chronic kidney disease progression. The capacity of S100A4 to influence both stromal cell behavior and immune recruitment makes it a plausible contributor to fibrogenic microenvironments in the injured kidney. Its role in angiogenesis may also intersect with capillary remodeling and hypoxia-driven disease progression.[PubMed:20519440](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20519440) [PubMed:8051043](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8051043) [PubMed:20103644](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20103644) 

In addition to local renal inflammation, systemic oxidative and vascular stress may also shape disease progression.

PON1 is relevant to kidney disease primarily because oxidative stress and lipoprotein dysfunction are major contributors to cardiovascular and renal injury in chronic kidney disease. By protecting LDL from oxidative modification, PON1 may help limit vascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and atherogenic processes that are closely linked to reduced renal perfusion and CKD-associated cardiovascular burden. Although not kidney-specific in the annotation, this antioxidant and vasculoprotective function is highly pertinent to the systemic complications that both accompany and worsen kidney disease.

Vascular injury in the kidney is also tightly linked to coagulation pathway activity.

F9 is relevant to kidney disease because dysregulated coagulation is increasingly recognized as a contributor to glomerular and microvascular injury. Activation of coagulation pathways can promote fibrin deposition, endothelial dysfunction, and thrombotic complications in the renal circulation, while abnormalities of hemostasis are common in nephrotic syndrome, inflammatory kidney disease, and advanced CKD. Although Factor IX is not kidney-specific, its central role in clotting makes it important in the context of renal thromboinflammation and microvascular compromise.

This hemostatic theme is further strengthened by a protein with a particularly direct connection to renal microvascular thrombosis.

ADAMTS13 is particularly important for kidney disease because impaired regulation of von Willebrand factor can lead to platelet-rich microthrombi, a hallmark of thrombotic microangiopathy. The kidney is one of the organs most vulnerable to microvascular thrombosis, and ADAMTS13 deficiency or dysfunction can therefore contribute to acute renal injury through glomerular and arteriolar occlusion. Even outside classical thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, the ADAMTS13-vWF axis is relevant to endothelial injury, inflammation, and renal microcirculatory integrity. This makes ADAMTS13 a highly meaningful vascular-hemostatic factor in nephrology.

Shifting from vascular processes to tissue architecture, calcium-dependent adhesion molecules may also be relevant to renal remodeling.

CDH2 is potentially relevant to kidney disease because cadherin-mediated adhesion is fundamental to epithelial integrity, tissue architecture, and cell-cell communication. Although the provided annotation emphasizes neural functions, the core property of calcium-dependent intercellular adhesion is broadly important in epithelial organs such as the kidney. Loss or remodeling of adhesion programs is a key feature of tubular injury, epithelial dedifferentiation, and fibrosis. Therefore, CDH2 may be of interest as a marker or mediator of altered cell-cell adhesion in renal tissue remodeling, even though the current entry does not specify renal roles directly.[PubMed:11433297](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11433297) [PubMed:17988630](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17988630) [PubMed:25253890](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25253890) [PubMed:2762814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2762814) [PubMed:9655503](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9655503) [PubMed:24952463](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24952463) [PubMed:26750727](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26750727) 

Extracellular matrix assembly and vascular adaptation are also reflected in additional matricellular proteins in the enriched set.

SMOC2 is relevant to kidney disease because matrix assembly, endothelial behavior, and angiogenesis are central to both repair and fibrosis in the injured kidney. Aberrant endothelial proliferation and migration can influence capillary remodeling, while altered matrix assembly contributes to interstitial scarring and changes in glomerular structure. A matricellular protein with these properties may therefore participate in the balance between adaptive repair and maladaptive fibrotic remodeling. SMOC2 is especially interesting in diseases characterized by microvascular rarefaction and extracellular matrix expansion.

Finally, another extracellular matrix-associated regulator may connect chronic stress responses with vascular and interstitial remodeling in the kidney.

THBS4 is potentially important in kidney disease because it integrates extracellular matrix remodeling, vascular inflammation, and stress adaptation. In the kidney, these processes are central to chronic injury progression, particularly in fibrotic and ischemic settings. The annotation suggests that THBS4 can reshape the extracellular environment after tissue damage and regulate inflammatory vascular responses, both of which are highly relevant to tubulointerstitial fibrosis and microvascular dysfunction. As a matricellular regulator of injury responses, THBS4 may contribute to how renal tissue adapts—or maladapts—to chronic stress.

### Neutrophil degranulation (REAC:R-HSA-6798695) 

Neutrophil degranulation is a core effector process of the innate immune response in which neutrophils, after sensing inflammatory, infectious, or tissue injury signals, mobilize and release the contents of specialized intracellular granules into phagosomes or the extracellular space. These granules contain proteolytic enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, oxidant-generating machinery, cationic proteins, and inflammatory mediators that are organized across several granule classes, including primary granules, secondary granules, tertiary granules, and secretory vesicles. Through degranulation, neutrophils can rapidly kill pathogens, remodel extracellular matrix, amplify leukocyte recruitment, activate endothelial cells, and shape local inflammatory responses. However, excessive or dysregulated degranulation can damage host tissues by promoting endothelial injury, increasing vascular permeability, degrading basement membranes, inducing oxidative stress, and exposing autoantigens. In the kidney, these effects are particularly important because the glomerular filtration barrier, tubular epithelium, interstitium, and microvasculature are highly susceptible to protease- and oxidant-mediated injury. Thus, neutrophil degranulation represents a biologically plausible mechanism linking systemic or local inflammation to acute and chronic renal damage.  

Against this biological background, the potential relevance of this pathway to kidney disease can be considered within established principles of renal immunopathology. Although no specific publications were provided for direct citation, the relationship between neutrophil degranulation and kidney disease can be understood from established renal immunopathology. In kidney disease, especially in inflammatory forms of glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury, neutrophils are recruited to the renal microvasculature and tissue by chemotactic signals generated by endothelial cells, resident immune cells, complement activation, and injured parenchymal cells. Once activated, neutrophils undergo degranulation and release proteases, myeloperoxidase, elastase, matrix-degrading enzymes, and other cytotoxic mediators that can directly injure glomerular endothelial cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, and tubular epithelial cells. This process can disrupt the glomerular filtration barrier, promote protein leakage, intensify capillary necrosis, and aggravate interstitial inflammation and fibrosis. Degranulation products may also enhance thrombosis, activate complement and coagulation pathways, and sustain a feed-forward inflammatory loop that worsens renal dysfunction. In acute kidney injury, neutrophil granule contents can contribute to ischemia-reperfusion damage and microvascular congestion, whereas in chronic kidney disease persistent low-grade neutrophil activation may support progressive tissue remodeling and scarring. In autoimmune kidney disorders, neutrophil granule proteins can serve as targets or amplifiers of pathogenic immune responses, further linking this pathway to severe renal injury. Therefore, neutrophil degranulation is best viewed as a double-edged biological program whose antimicrobial function becomes pathogenic when excessive, prolonged, or misdirected within the kidney.  

This conceptual framework is further supported by the enrichment results observed in the present analysis. There were 89 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of neutrophil degranulation, indicating a substantial convergence of disease-related molecular signals on an innate immune effector program that is highly relevant to renal injury. This protein set size of 89 supports a broad and biologically meaningful enrichment pattern rather than an isolated signal, and it is consistent with the concept that protease release, oxidant generation, extracellular matrix remodeling, endothelial activation, and inflammatory amplification collectively contribute to damage in the glomerular filtration barrier, tubular epithelium, interstitium, and renal microvasculature in kidney disease. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 89 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for interactive network inspection and further analysis.

![PPI Network](imgs/fe809752-8385-45be-be8849-af3917deb23e.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=3B03DFC6F58FFB23)

Building on this pathway-level enrichment, the following proteins may help clarify which biological processes are contributing to the observed signal. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

BST2 is particularly relevant to kidney disease because renal injury frequently intersects with innate antiviral and interferon-driven inflammation, especially in virus-associated nephropathies and inflammatory glomerular disorders. Its core function as a broad antiviral tethering factor suggests a role in restricting viral dissemination within renal tissue, while its additional capacity to regulate NF-kappa-B signaling and plasmacytoid dendritic cell interferon responses places it at the center of inflammatory amplification and feedback control. These properties are mechanistically important because excessive type one interferon signaling and NF-kappa-B activation are well-established contributors to glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury. Moreover, the reported inhibition of MMP14-dependent proteolytic activity and downstream effects on cell growth and migration may be relevant to renal remodeling and fibrosis, processes that depend on matrix turnover and epithelial or stromal cell motility. Thus, BST2 stands out as a protein linking antiviral defense, immune regulation, and tissue remodeling, all of which are highly pertinent to kidney pathology.[PubMed:18200009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18200009) [PubMed:18342597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18342597) [PubMed:19036818](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19036818) [PubMed:19879838](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19879838) [PubMed:20019814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20019814) [PubMed:20399176](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20399176) [PubMed:20419159](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20419159) [PubMed:20940320](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20940320) [PubMed:21529378](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21529378) [PubMed:22520941](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22520941) [PubMed:22065321](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22065321) [PubMed:19564354](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19564354) [PubMed:26172439](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26172439) [PubMed:23028328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23028328)  

A closely related theme is proximal innate immune sensing, which may be especially relevant in kidney disorders with infectious or sterile inflammatory triggers. CD14 is one of the most compelling proteins in this list for kidney disease because it is a proximal mediator of innate immune activation in response to bacterial products, a pathway central to sepsis-associated acute kidney injury, pyelonephritis, and sterile inflammatory amplification in chronic kidney disease. Through lipopolysaccharide recognition and toll-like receptor four signaling, CD14 promotes NF-kappa-B activation and cytokine release, processes that drive endothelial dysfunction, tubular injury, leukocyte recruitment, and microvascular inflammation in the kidney. Its additional role in recognizing mycobacterial and lipopeptide ligands broadens its relevance to infection-related renal injury. The ability of CD14 to bind electronegative low-density lipoprotein also suggests a connection to inflammation linked to dyslipidemia, which is common in chronic kidney disease and may aggravate vascular and glomerular damage. Overall, CD14 is important because it integrates pathogen sensing with inflammatory signaling pathways that are directly implicated in both acute and chronic renal injury.[PubMed:16148141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16148141) [PubMed:15895089](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15895089) [PubMed:8612135](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8612135) [PubMed:19362712](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19362712)  

Extending this innate recognition framework, additional lectin-like receptors may also contribute to inflammatory kidney injury through related signaling mechanisms. CLEC4D is relevant to kidney disease because it participates in innate immune recognition of microbial ligands and drives inflammatory programs that can influence infection-associated renal injury and immune-mediated kidney inflammation. Activation of the SYK-CARD9-NF-kappa-B axis is especially notable, as this pathway is implicated in myeloid-cell activation, cytokine production, and T helper seventeen polarization, all of which can contribute to renal tissue damage when excessive or sustained. In the setting of fungal or mycobacterial infection, CLEC4D-dependent signaling may help protect the host, but in parallel it may intensify inflammatory injury within the kidney. Its endocytic and antigen-uptake functions further suggest a role in coordinating local immune activation and adaptive responses. This makes CLEC4D a biologically plausible contributor to infection-triggered kidney injury and to inflammatory crosstalk between innate and adaptive immunity in renal disease.[PubMed:23602766](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23602766) [PubMed:23911656](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23911656) [PubMed:14971047](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971047)  

Within the same general category of receptor-driven inflammation, CLEC5A may be relevant because it illustrates how strong cytokine responses can contribute to organ injury even when direct renal infection is not the primary event. CLEC5A stands out because it exemplifies how pathogen recognition can provoke damaging inflammation independently of direct infection. This is highly relevant to kidney disease in systemic viral infections, where cytokine-driven endothelial injury, capillary leak, and inflammatory tubular damage can contribute to acute kidney injury. By triggering TYROBP-dependent inflammatory signaling in macrophages, CLEC5A may amplify systemic and local cytokine responses that secondarily affect renal perfusion, glomerular permeability, and tubulointerstitial integrity. Although the provided annotation is focused on dengue, the broader mechanistic principle—innate receptor-driven hyperinflammation causing organ injury—is directly applicable to kidney pathology in severe viral disease.[PubMed:18496526](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18496526) [PubMed:21566123](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21566123)  

Another related process is complement-linked inflammatory activation, which is often prominent in glomerular disease. FCN1 is of considerable interest in kidney disease because complement activation is a major pathogenic mechanism in many glomerular disorders, including infection-related glomerulonephritis and complement-mediated inflammatory injury. By initiating the lectin pathway upon recognition of microbial carbohydrate structures, FCN1 may contribute to renal inflammation through complement deposition, leukocyte recruitment, and endothelial or mesangial injury. Its ability to induce interleukin eight secretion through monocyte activation further supports a role in neutrophil-rich inflammatory responses, which are often observed in acute renal inflammatory lesions. Therefore, FCN1 is important as a bridge between innate pathogen sensing, complement activation, and inflammatory recruitment, all of which are mechanistically relevant to kidney injury.  

In parallel with inflammatory signaling, pathways governing matrix interaction and tissue remodeling may also help explain the renal relevance of the enriched protein set. ITGAV is one of the strongest kidney disease candidates in this list because alpha-V integrins are central regulators of extracellular matrix interactions, angiogenesis, wound repair, and, importantly, transforming growth factor beta activation. Transforming growth factor beta signaling is a canonical driver of renal fibrosis, promoting fibroblast activation, matrix deposition, epithelial dysfunction, and progressive loss of kidney function. The ability of ITGAV-containing integrins to release active transforming growth factor beta one from latent complexes provides a direct mechanistic link to chronic kidney disease progression and fibrotic remodeling. In addition, its roles in adhesion, migration, and vascular biology suggest relevance to glomerular and tubulointerstitial remodeling, capillary rarefaction, and maladaptive repair after injury. For these reasons, ITGAV stands out as a highly plausible mediator of fibrogenic and structural changes in diseased kidneys.[PubMed:10025398](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10025398) [PubMed:9827803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9827803) [PubMed:25127859](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25127859) [PubMed:11323698](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11323698) [PubMed:24935931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24935931)  

Because neutrophil degranulation is tightly linked to lipid mediator production and inflammatory cell recruitment, enzymes that regulate these mediators may also be important to consider. LTA4H is highly relevant to kidney disease because it occupies a pivotal position in lipid mediator biology, balancing pro-inflammatory and pro-resolving pathways. Its generation of leukotriene B4 can promote neutrophil recruitment and activation, processes that are important in acute kidney injury, immune-complex nephritis, and other inflammatory renal disorders. Conversely, its aminopeptidase activity may limit inflammation by degrading PGP, and its involvement in resolvin E1 biosynthesis suggests a role in inflammation resolution. This duality is particularly important in the kidney, where the extent and duration of leukocyte infiltration often determine whether injury resolves or progresses to fibrosis. Therefore, LTA4H is notable as a mediator that may influence both inflammatory damage and recovery in renal disease.[PubMed:1881903](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1881903) [PubMed:9287304](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9287304) [PubMed:20813919](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20813919)  

A complementary aspect of renal injury involves intracellular metabolic stress, particularly disturbances in lysosomal and lipid homeostasis. NPC2 is relevant to kidney disease because lysosomal lipid handling and cholesterol trafficking are increasingly recognized as important determinants of tubular cell health, macrophage activation, and renal fibrosis. Defective cholesterol egress from lysosomes can promote lipotoxic stress, organelle dysfunction, and inflammatory activation, all of which are implicated in chronic kidney disease and proteinuric nephropathies. Renal tubular epithelial cells are particularly vulnerable to metabolic and lysosomal stress, and altered sterol trafficking may aggravate maladaptive responses to injury. Thus, NPC2 stands out as a protein linking intracellular lipid homeostasis to mechanisms of renal cell dysfunction and chronic disease progression.[PubMed:12591949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12591949) [PubMed:17018531](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17018531) [PubMed:21315718](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21315718) [PubMed:26296895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26296895)  

This metabolic dimension is also reflected at the level of oxidative lipid recognition and vascular inflammation. OLR1 is especially important in kidney disease because it directly links dyslipidemia, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and inflammation—core features of both diabetic kidney disease and progressive chronic kidney disease. By binding oxidized low-density lipoprotein and activating reactive oxygen species-dependent NF-kappa-B signaling, OLR1 can promote vascular inflammation, apoptosis, and impaired nitric oxide bioavailability, all of which are highly relevant to glomerular endothelial injury and intrarenal vascular dysfunction. Its ability to recognize advanced glycation end products further strengthens its relevance to diabetic nephropathy, where glycoxidative stress contributes to mesangial expansion, albuminuria, and fibrosis. In addition, its leukocyte-adhesion and bacterial recognition functions suggest broader roles in inflammatory recruitment and infection-associated renal injury. Overall, OLR1 stands out as a strong mechanistic candidate at the intersection of metabolic and inflammatory kidney disease.  

Alongside these direct inflammatory and metabolic mechanisms, endocrine and cytoskeletal regulation may provide a more indirect but still relevant connection to renal pathology. PTPRN2 is noteworthy in relation to kidney disease primarily because of its role in insulin vesicle homeostasis and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, which links it indirectly to diabetic kidney disease, the leading cause of chronic kidney failure. Perturbation of insulin secretion contributes to systemic hyperglycemia, which in turn drives glomerular hyperfiltration, oxidative stress, advanced glycation, inflammation, and fibrosis. Beyond this endocrine connection, its regulation of phosphatidylinositol four, five-bisphosphate and actin dynamics suggests possible relevance to cell motility and cytoskeletal organization, processes that are also critical in podocyte biology and epithelial integrity. Therefore, although not a classical renal protein, PTPRN2 may have meaningful disease relevance through metabolic control and phosphoinositide-dependent cellular architecture.[PubMed:21732083](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21732083) [PubMed:15220191](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15220191) [PubMed:16418280](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16418280) [PubMed:16269463](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16269463) [PubMed:19019914](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19019914) [PubMed:12364328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12364328)  

Returning to soluble mediators of innate immunity, PTX3 may be relevant because it sits at the interface of host defense, inflammatory regulation, and tissue injury. PTX3 is highly relevant to kidney disease because it is a key soluble mediator of innate immunity and inflammation, two processes that are central to both acute and chronic renal injury. Its involvement in pathogen resistance suggests importance in infection-associated kidney disease, while its role in inflammatory regulation and clearance of self-components is directly pertinent to immune-complex handling, sterile inflammation, and tissue repair. In the kidney, dysregulated innate immune activation can worsen glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury, whereas impaired clearance of damaged material may sustain chronic inflammation. PTX3 therefore stands out as a plausible marker and mediator of renal inflammatory responses, particularly in settings where innate immunity and tissue damage intersect.  

Another potentially important downstream consequence of chronic injury is extracellular matrix reorganization. QSOX1 is particularly interesting in kidney disease because extracellular matrix organization is a central determinant of glomerular basement membrane integrity, tubular basement membrane stability, and interstitial fibrosis. Its role in disulfide bond formation in extracellular proteins and in laminin incorporation suggests direct relevance to matrix assembly and remodeling. In the kidney, aberrant matrix deposition and altered adhesion are hallmarks of chronic injury and fibrosis, while basement membrane abnormalities contribute to filtration barrier dysfunction. Because QSOX1 influences both matrix composition and cell migratory behavior, it may participate in maladaptive repair responses that drive chronic kidney disease progression.[PubMed:17331072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17331072) [PubMed:18393449](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18393449) [PubMed:23704371](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23704371) [PubMed:23867277](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23867277) [PubMed:30367560](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30367560) [PubMed:22801504](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22801504)  

In addition to matrix remodeling, nucleic acid sensing pathways may represent another route through which innate immunity contributes to renal inflammation. RNASET2 is relevant to kidney disease because it connects nucleic acid sensing with innate immune activation, a pathway increasingly implicated in autoimmune and inflammatory renal disorders. By generating ribonucleic acid degradation products that stimulate toll-like receptor eight and toll-like receptor seven pathways, RNASET2 may promote cytokine production and interferon responses that contribute to glomerular and tubulointerstitial inflammation. This is particularly important in diseases characterized by heightened endosomal nucleic acid sensing, where exaggerated innate immune activation can damage renal tissue. Its additional role in mitochondrial ribonucleic acid turnover is also noteworthy, since mitochondrial stress and release of mitochondrial nucleic acids are increasingly recognized as drivers of sterile inflammation in kidney injury. Thus, RNASET2 stands out as a mechanistic link between ribonucleic acid metabolism and inflammatory kidney disease.[PubMed:31778653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31778653) [PubMed:38697119](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38697119) [PubMed:28730546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28730546) [PubMed:30184494](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184494) [PubMed:30385512](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30385512)  

Cellular stress responses within secretory and metabolically active renal cells provide a further layer of possible relevance. TXNDC5 is important for kidney disease because endoplasmic reticulum proteostasis and redox homeostasis are major determinants of renal cell survival under metabolic, inflammatory, and hypoxic stress. As a protein disulfide isomerase, TXNDC5 supports oxidative folding in the endoplasmic reticulum, and dysregulation of this process can contribute to endoplasmic reticulum stress, unfolded protein responses, and ultimately tubular or glomerular cell injury. These mechanisms are highly relevant in diabetic kidney disease, proteinuric states, and fibrotic progression, where secretory burden and oxidative stress are increased. Its reported ability to reduce insulin disulfide bonds also links it indirectly to metabolic regulation, further increasing its relevance to diabetic renal pathology.[PubMed:12930873](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12930873) [PubMed:14971039](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14971039)  

Lipid handling remains a recurring theme in kidney disease biology, and FABP5 may fit within this broader framework. FABP5 is relevant to kidney disease because lipid dysregulation and inflammatory lipid signaling are major contributors to renal injury, particularly in obesity-related kidney disease and diabetic nephropathy. By trafficking fatty acids and bioactive lipids, FABP5 may influence cellular lipid accumulation, nuclear receptor activation, and metabolic adaptation in renal cells. Its capacity to modulate NF-kappa-B signaling and prostaglandin E2 biosynthesis further connects it to inflammatory pathways that can exacerbate glomerular and tubulointerstitial damage. Since renal lipotoxicity is increasingly recognized as a driver of chronic kidney disease progression, FABP5 stands out as a plausible mediator linking altered lipid handling to inflammation and survival signaling in the kidney.[PubMed:12540600](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12540600) [PubMed:8608126](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8608126) [PubMed:17512406](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17512406) [PubMed:29531087](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29531087) [PubMed:29440395](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29440395)  

Related to oxidative and metabolic stress, heme handling may also be important in specific forms of renal injury. HMOX2 is potentially relevant to kidney disease because heme metabolism is a critical determinant of oxidative injury, especially in hemolysis-associated and ischemic renal damage. The enzymatic degradation of heme can reduce the toxicity of free heme, while generating bioactive products such as carbon monoxide and biliverdin and bilirubin that may influence oxidative stress, vascular tone, and cytoprotection. In the kidney, where tubular cells are highly susceptible to oxidative and heme-mediated injury, this pathway may modulate the balance between injury and adaptation. Accordingly, HMOX2 stands out as a candidate relevant to redox regulation and protection from heme-driven renal damage.  

Finally, the intensity and persistence of renal inflammation are also shaped by inhibitory immune checkpoints, which may restrain tissue-damaging responses. LAIR1 is relevant to kidney disease because immune inhibitory receptors are essential for preventing excessive tissue-damaging inflammation, particularly in autoimmune and chronic inflammatory renal disorders. Its broad suppression of lymphocyte activation, cytokine production, and NF-kappa-B signaling suggests a protective role against sustained immune-mediated renal injury. The induction of transforming growth factor beta and inhibition of dendritic cell differentiation indicate additional effects on immune polarization and antigen presentation, processes that can shape glomerular and interstitial inflammation. In diseases such as lupus nephritis or other immune-mediated nephropathies, altered LAIR1 signaling could influence whether immune responses remain controlled or become pathogenic. Thus, LAIR1 stands out as a regulator of immune tolerance and inflammatory restraint in contexts directly relevant to kidney disease.

### phosphatidylcholine metabolic process (GO:0046470) 

The phosphatidylcholine metabolic process comprises the synthesis, remodeling, interconversion, transport, and degradation of phosphatidylcholines, which are major structural glycerophospholipids of eukaryotic membranes. Phosphatidylcholines are essential for the biophysical organization of plasma membranes and intracellular organelles, where they influence membrane fluidity, curvature, lipid packing, vesicular trafficking, and the assembly of membrane-associated protein complexes. Their metabolism includes de novo biosynthesis through choline incorporation, reacylation and remodeling reactions that alter fatty acyl chain composition, and catabolic cleavage by phospholipases that generate biologically active lipid mediators such as lysophosphatidylcholine, diacylglycerol, and phosphatidic acid. Through these reactions, phosphatidylcholine metabolism contributes not only to membrane homeostasis but also to cell signaling, lipoprotein handling, oxidative stress responses, inflammatory activation, apoptosis, and organelle integrity, particularly in mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum. Because the kidney depends on highly specialized epithelial membranes, polarized transport systems, and tightly regulated responses to metabolic and inflammatory stress, maintenance of phosphatidylcholine homeostasis is likely to be important for normal renal structure and function.

With this biological context in mind, the current evidence base should be interpreted cautiously. No relevant publications were provided in the input, so a publication-based analysis specific to kidney disease cannot be performed and no direct literature-supported conclusion should be asserted. On a mechanistic basis, however, disturbance of the phosphatidylcholine metabolic process could plausibly contribute to kidney disease because renal cells, especially tubular epithelial cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, and glomerular endothelial cells, rely on intact membrane composition for filtration barrier maintenance, solute transport, mitochondrial function, and resistance to inflammatory and oxidative injury. Altered phosphatidylcholine synthesis or remodeling may change membrane properties and organelle stability, while increased phosphatidylcholine breakdown may elevate lysophosphatidylcholine and related lipid products that can promote inflammation, cell stress, and fibrotic signaling. In addition, dysregulated phosphatidylcholine handling may interact with lipid accumulation, lipoprotein abnormalities, and cellular injury pathways that are commonly observed in chronic kidney disease and acute kidney injury. Nevertheless, in the absence of the requested publications, these links should be regarded as biologically plausible interpretations rather than evidence-supported conclusions for this specific pathway in kidney disease.

This cautious mechanistic interpretation is broadly consistent with the enrichment result observed in the present analysis. There were 13 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the phosphatidylcholine metabolic process. This enrichment is biologically plausible because phosphatidylcholine metabolism spans multiple quantitatively important cellular functions, including synthesis, remodeling, interconversion, transport, and degradation, and these processes collectively regulate membrane composition, vesicular trafficking, inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses, apoptosis, and organelle stability in renal cells. Given that the kidney relies on highly specialized epithelial membranes, polarized transport architecture, and sustained metabolic homeostasis, an enrichment signal involving 13 proteins supports the interpretation that disruption of phosphatidylcholine balance may contribute meaningfully to kidney disease pathophysiology.

To further contextualize these enriched proteins, the network-level relationships are shown below. Building on this network overview, the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis are introduced below in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, ENPP2 stands out as highly relevant to kidney disease because its core enzymatic product, LPA, is a well-established signaling lipid that regulates processes central to renal pathobiology, including cell migration, proliferation, vascular remodeling, inflammation, and tissue fibrosis. The most important feature is that ENPP2 is secreted and acts in extracellular fluids to generate LPA from lysophosphatidylcholine, thereby amplifying paracrine signaling in injured tissues (PubMed:12354767, PubMed:14500380, PubMed:15769751, PubMed:26371182, PubMed:27754931). This is particularly meaningful in the kidney, where maladaptive extracellular signaling contributes to glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury. Its reported angiogenic activity, including stimulation of smooth muscle cell migration and microtubule formation, suggests possible relevance to renal microvascular remodeling, a major determinant of chronic kidney disease progression (PubMed:11559573). ENPP2-mediated promotion of cell motility, including melanoma cell migration through G protein-dependent mechanisms, further supports a broader role in migratory signaling pathways that may also influence mesangial cells, fibroblasts, inflammatory cells, and tubular epithelial responses during kidney injury (PubMed:1733949). In addition, the requirement of ENPP2 for LPA production in activated platelets links it to thrombo-inflammatory signaling, which is increasingly recognized in glomerular disease and vascular complications of kidney disease (PubMed:21393252). Although the provided annotations do not directly mention renal phenotypes, the combination of extracellular LPA generation, angiogenesis, motility regulation, and probable roles in proliferation makes ENPP2 a particularly compelling candidate for involvement in kidney disease mechanisms such as fibrosis, proteinuric injury, vascular dysfunction, and progression of chronic kidney disease.[PubMed:12354767](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12354767) [PubMed:14500380](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14500380) [PubMed:15769751](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15769751) [PubMed:26371182](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26371182) [PubMed:27754931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27754931) [PubMed:12176993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12176993) [PubMed:11559573](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11559573) [PubMed:1733949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1733949) [PubMed:21393252](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21393252)

### Matrix metalloproteinases (WP:WP129) 

Matrix metalloproteinases are a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that degrade and remodel components of the extracellular matrix, including collagens, laminins, elastin, fibronectin, and proteoglycans. Beyond structural matrix turnover, these enzymes also process cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, cell-surface receptors, and adhesion molecules, thereby influencing inflammation, cell migration, angiogenesis, epithelial integrity, and tissue repair. Their activity is tightly controlled at multiple levels, including gene transcription, secretion as inactive precursor proteins, extracellular activation, compartmentalization, and inhibition by endogenous tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases. Physiologically, balanced matrix metalloproteinase activity is essential for organ development, wound healing, and maintenance of basement membranes and interstitial architecture. Pathologically, dysregulated matrix metalloproteinase expression or activation can drive excessive matrix degradation, abnormal matrix accumulation through maladaptive remodeling, inflammatory cell recruitment, and fibrotic progression. In the kidney, where glomerular basement membrane integrity, tubular basement membrane stability, mesangial matrix homeostasis, and interstitial extracellular matrix composition are central to filtration and nephron function, perturbation of matrix metalloproteinase signaling has the potential to alter barrier permeability, promote inflammatory injury, and reshape the balance between repair and fibrosis.

With this biological framework in mind, the relevance of the pathway to kidney disease can be interpreted at the pathway level, while remaining cautious because no publication set was provided for direct evidence synthesis. No relevant publications were provided in the input, and therefore a publication-based pathway-to-disease analysis cannot be directly derived from the supplied evidence set. Nevertheless, based on established biological understanding of the matrix metalloproteinase pathway, this pathway appears highly relevant to kidney disease because renal injury is fundamentally accompanied by extracellular matrix remodeling, basement membrane disruption, inflammation, and fibrosis. In glomerular disease, altered matrix metalloproteinase activity may contribute to degradation of the glomerular basement membrane and mesangial matrix remodeling, which could impair filtration barrier function and favor protein leakage. In tubulointerstitial injury, matrix metalloproteinases may promote leukocyte infiltration and epithelial damage through proteolytic processing of matrix and inflammatory mediators, while persistent dysregulation may also facilitate fibrotic remodeling by disturbing the normal balance between matrix synthesis and matrix degradation. Importantly, the role of matrix metalloproteinases in kidney disease is context dependent: insufficient activity may favor extracellular matrix accumulation and scarring, whereas excessive or mislocalized activity may intensify tissue destruction and inflammatory injury. Thus, the pathway may be viewed as a central regulator of renal matrix homeostasis whose imbalance could contribute to both acute tissue damage and chronic progression toward fibrosis and loss of kidney function. Because no source publications were supplied, these conclusions should be regarded as pathway-level biological interpretation rather than a formal evidence synthesis tied to the provided citation list.

Consistent with this pathway-level interpretation, the enrichment results provide a more quantitative indication of kidney disease relevance. There were 13 kidney disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing matrix metalloproteinases as a family of zinc-dependent endopeptidases that mediate extracellular matrix degradation and remodeling, with direct relevance to collagen, laminin, elastin, fibronectin, and proteoglycan turnover, as well as broader regulation of cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, cell-surface receptors, and adhesion molecules. This protein set of 13 highlights a quantitatively focused enrichment signal centered on extracellular matrix homeostasis, inflammatory regulation, tissue repair, and fibrotic remodeling, all of which are biologically central to kidney disease because glomerular basement membrane integrity, tubular basement membrane stability, mesangial matrix balance, and interstitial extracellular matrix composition are essential determinants of filtration function and nephron preservation. In this context, the enrichment of 13 proteins in this pathway supports a disease-relevant functional theme in which altered metalloproteinase activity may shift the balance between physiological repair and pathological fibrosis, promote inflammatory cell recruitment, and modify barrier permeability through maladaptive remodeling of renal structural compartments.
